By combining theoretical transport modeling with actual data from experiments, we establish a specific single-electron energy spectrum for the nanotubes. Furthermore, our analysis of electronic conductance under various temperatures reveals an intense, temperature-dependent peak. Recent research indicates that deep neural networks demonstrate consistent performance across various domains, despite being trained on limited data and when testing is done on unseen domains. This issue is complex, involving multiple factors. We challenge two prevailing assumptions about this phenomenon: the idea that similar data leads to similar outputs, and the notion that neural networks inherently possess domain-agnostic capabilities. Through thorough examination, our investigation uncovers that while theories may explain some non-transferable cases, a considerable number of domains with limited data remain unaccounted for. We devise a method to evaluate whether data sets are transferable or not, and provide practical applications for this new perspective on representational capabilities. Our research also shows that data transformation, model adaptation, and training data selection can all be leveraged to enhance data transferability, which in turn improves overall model performance. We base our approaches on an understanding of our method's underlying principles, and conduct experiments to test their effectiveness in comparison to established methods, revealing notable improvements as a result. Our findings and associated code are made available for future reference at https://github.com/whwu/Transferability. We also discuss how the concept of transferability relates to broader theoretical considerations. This research ultimately aims to contribute a more nuanced understanding of the complex issue of consistent neural network performance across different domains. We hope that our insights and techniques will facilitate the creation of more adaptable and versatile deep neural networks. Furthermore, we aim to make accessible simpler and more automated methods for achieving robust and highly generalizable models. Such advancements could significantly reduce the time and computational resources needed for model development and acceleration on GPU, and potentially lead to breakthroughs in areas such as multi-task learning and data efficiency. This paper introduces a model and algorithm for a dial-a-ride problem with limited capacity vehicles, inspired by real-world applications in Paris's metropolitan area. The model incorporates various key factors such as exact dates, vehicle limitations, multiple depots, and a flexible time windows policy. A high-performance solution has been developed in the form of a hybrid Branch-and-Trim algorithm, combining Branch-and-Bound and branch-and-cut techniques. Key features of this method involve efficient model reduction, which reduces solution time without compromising vehicle efficiency. Additionally, high-quality initial lower bounds obtained through heuristics enhance the overall performance of the algorithm. The proposed approach achieves exceptional results, with high quality solutions found within short processing times for large-scale instances. Notably, this method outperforms other dial-a-ride solutions by a significant margin, with reductions of up to 50% in vehicle usage in tested cases. Several case studies and numerical analysis have been conducted to evaluate the effectiveness of this new approach. As part of an operational platform since 2017, this method has played a crucial role in planning dial-a-ride services in Paris's metropolitan area. With over 2 million users and a fleet of nearly 21,000 vehicles, this method has been instrumental in shaping public policy and social programs aimed at promoting mobility and urban living. As such, this method has far-reaching implications for urban planning and public transportation systems. To facilitate further research and development, the dial-a-ride problem source code has been made publicly available on GitHub. With this code, researchers and practitioners can build upon and improve this powerful algorithm, ultimately leading to even better solutions. Similarly, the Paris metropolitan area dial-a-ride problem (PMDRP) can be accessed through its GitHub page. This study explores enhancing the effectiveness of e-commerce product retrievals using information-aware pretraining of convolutional neural networks (CNNs). We propose the Knowledge-Aware CNN (KACNN), which leverages the integrated power of text, image, and semantics to better comprehend product characteristics. By combining the recognition of semantic information and multi-modal signals with a unified text-image semantics knowledge recognition, the KACNN framework is able to effectively integrate these components for robust e-commerce search. Furthermore, our framework demonstrates strong adaptability when dealing with single-modal and weak semantic information searches. Extensive experiments validate the KACNN's capability to efficiently retrieve relevant products from a vast database. Unlike prior research, our study focuses on the recognition of semantic information in e-commerce product searches. We propose a two-phase multi-modal pretraining approach for robust e-commerce search. The KACNN pretrains models on two key tasks: text-image multi-modal search and semantic information recognition. The pretrained KACNN can be fine-tuned for various e-commerce search applications, encompassing multi-modal and weak semantic information searches. We test the efficacy of KACNN on four datasets and observe significant improvements in search accuracy. Notably, our KACNN model achieves a remarkable 0.44 mean average precision at 10 (MAP@10) boost in deep fashion image search, whereas incorporating recognized semantic information yields a 0.10 point enhancement. These results motivate further investigation of pretraining the KACNN for a wide array of e-commerce applications. The related code and models for the KACNN are available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/whwu95/KACNN.git. Our study's other findings and associated data are hosted on the https://github.com/whwu95/LearnableSeeds.git platform. The research was implemented in a TensorFlow environment. The data was collected from the following sources: Amazon Ground Truth, Google Product Dataset, DeepFashion, and Stanford Product Search. The research was disseminated at the ACM Multimedia 2020. Autoregressive models are commonly used for time-series analysis, particularly when forecasting future values. In the case of Alzheimer's disease, forecasting key time-series variables like cortisol levels, essential for daily routines, can be crucial. We introduce a deep learning approach to forecast cortisol levels using the Deep InfoMax algorithm. This algorithm uses unsupervised techniques to capture nuanced cortisol patterns, which are then incorporated into a autoregressive model for accurate prediction. We propose a new performance metric, the Dynamic Recovery Rate, to evaluate model effectiveness in mimicking the cortisol rhythm and assessing recovery dynamics. Our method achieves optimal results, outperforming the baseline model in multiple dimensions, including a significant 91.9% improvement in the Dynamic Recovery Rate. We also demonstrate model generalization, achieving a Dynamic Recovery Rate of 67.1% on an entirely new population. These findings have significant implications for clinical assessment, as they can be utilized in a step-down hemodynamic model to forecast cortisol levels and assess disease progression in Alzheimer's patients. Our model demonstrates exceptional performance, both in forecasting and recovery scenarios, and we hope its integration with additional clinical data will lead to a diagnosis support system. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/cookie911/Alzheimer_Forecast.git. Experimental results can be accessed at https://my.nocow.vn/Alzheimer_Forecast. We welcome community feedback to advance our work. The achievement of our model highlights its practical utility, and we believe its advancement has the potential to contribute to a diagnosis support system. Our model's success is expected to inspire future research in utility maximization and step-down identification, promoting the development of a diagnosis support system. The experimental results of our work are publicly available at https://my.nocow.vn/Alzheimer_Forecast/. Overall, the proposed notion and associated classification exhibit a high degree of universality, flexibility, and creativity. As medical AI models are deployed as real-world decision tools, accurately evaluating their performance becomes a critical concern. This work investigates non-parametric prediction assessment techniques, particularly those that can handle significant distribution changes, like model shifts during online testing and cross-dataset evaluations. We showcase the efficacy of conformal prediction analysis in tackling these challenges, highlighting its capabilities in handling complex testing scenarios. Furthermore, we contend that this approach offers the most suitable evaluation framework for AI models under substantial distribution changes. This work originates from a competition held on AI medical instrument performance assessment, emphasizing the need for reliable prediction assessment techniques in high-stakes medical AI applications. We participate in this challenge with a method based on conformal forecasting, which we detail and demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on various datasets, such as dataset splits, and across multiple distribution changes involving different datasets, medical labels, and medical AI models. Our results indicate that our method excels in robustness, balance, and accuracy, outperforming other competing methods. We ultimately achieve the top overall ranking and the top rank in robustness and balance for this challenge with our method. Our work is documented at a publicly accessible URL.

The utilization of drones in a military setting is becoming increasingly common, primarily in a reconnaissance role, despite their limited capabilities when compared to commercial drones. Given that military drones are still a relatively new concept, there is a shortage of information available on their specifications, a void that can be addressed by analyzing publicly accessible descriptions from websites and social media platforms. This research applies a combination of natural language processing techniques, including text extraction, entity recognition, and part-of-speech analysis, to gather insights into the development trajectory of military drones by examining the language used in descriptions and the semantic relationships between words. A significant discovery made through this analysis was the distinction between drones used for surveillance or combat, with the former typically consisting of a few manufacturers from Western countries and the latter comprising a larger pool of international manufacturers. Additionally, our analysis identified an alarming number of military drone-related incidents worldwide. A visualization tool was also developed to illustrate word associations related to military drone specifications. However, it is crucial to address the challenges and limitations inherent in this research, particularly those stemming from the subjectivity of text and the potential for underreporting or exaggeration of drone activities. Finally, we discuss potential applications and further research directions. The Lyman-$\alpha$ forest at high redshift provides a synthetic map of

luminous sources. It contains measurable absorption lines within the spectra 
of quasars that are characterized by complex redshift shifts. Although these 
redshifts, driven primarily by the peculiar motion of absorption line clouds, 
introduce significant random distortions, the associated fluctuations at small 
separations remain correlated. We precisely measure these fluctuations at 
separations ranging from 90,000 to 2.8 million light years and find them to be 
consistent with the predictions of a specific two-dimensional Gaussian 
probability distribution across a wide range of redshift from 2.2 to 4.7. 
Our precise measurement enables us to determine the cosmological parameters 
of the world with greater precision than through the traditional analysis of 
fluctuations at large scales. Notably, our results agree well with the latest 
data on the cosmological parameters, while the traditional method yields 
somewhat different values for certain parameters. We observed a deficit in

scale range. Our results suggest that the formation of structures occurs

Researchers at Fermilab have successfully observed the transfer of transverse and longitudinal beam emittances between two beams of different energies for the first time.  This achievement involved matching the beam momentum at the Switchyard, so that a low-energy beam and a high-energy beam were on the same trajectory.  By introducing a small imperfection in the switchyard, the emittance from one beam was transferred to the other.  This experiment marked a crucial milestone for the Proton Booster and Proton Source, using a low-energy beam to adjust the beam emittance.  The first experimental setup allowed the transfer of both transverse and longitudinal emittives, while future upgrades will allow the emittance to be adjusted.  The new technology also opens up possible applications in beam manipulation and in advanced accelerator concepts like the Fast Extraction and energy recovery.  The new capability was tested in a fully-integrated context in the Proton Source, the first time this had ever happened.  The successful experiment marked a major step forward for the construction of the Fermilab Upgrade Proton Source, and the results will have a wide range of applications.  The new emittance adjustment technique may also have a range of potential applications in various accelerator systems. In the context of a fully connected Boltzmann machine, which is a fundamental element of an unsupervised neural network, we examine the relationship between two measures of complexity: one based on latent variables and the other based on input data. Our analysis reveals a difference in behavior between these measures as the network further trains its parameters beyond achieving maximum likelihood estimation, indicating that the latent structure and the data pattern have contrasting complexities. Furthermore, the fluctuation of the data-based complexity is found to be inversely related to the network's width, implying that the amount of fluctuation and the size of the network are inversely proportional. Finally, the properties of these complexity measures are found to be analogous to those of the information bottleneck principle when applied to a Boltzmann machine in unsupervised learning settings. An extensive investigation was carried out with various parameter settings to solidify the results, which are presented in a reproducible and code-based manner. The resulting insights could offer a new perspective on the underlying mechanisms of an unservised neural network in its training process. The accompanying code can be accessed at https://github.com/moarbrew/ITCM.

In the analysis of microscopic images, experts combine findings from several
characteristics to identify objects. For instance, when categorizing white blood
cells, experts consider the size, shape, and structural features as well as the
overall cell shape. This requires integrating information from various sources
in a non-linear manner, which is typically challenging to accomplish in machine
learning models. Unlike human specialists, who can simply reassess images when
initially classified incorrectly, expert systems once trained rarely change their
classifications. This leads to a significant drawback: even though digital
microbiological tests are highly reliable when repeated, the results of automatic
classifiers are not. Furthermore, the interpretation of model predictions may not
be entirely accurate due to the lack of clear insight into the process. This study
investigates whether creating ensemble models can address these issues by
merging the predictions of several neural networks trained to identify general
cell characteristics, as well as specialized networks trained to classify different
types of blood cells. This approach involves combining information at both the
feature and output levels using methods such as hard voting, soft voting, and
weighted fusion. It also involves evaluating the performance of our models using
the human-labeled images that are part of the NIDSHC collection. This study
utilized 1,918 annotated images from the NIDSHC dataset and obtained the
following mean average precision scores: 0.6497 for the general model, 0. Dolnik
for the specific models, and 0.6496-0.8497 for the merged models. These
outcomes confirm that merging the predictions of multiple models improves their
accuracy and reduces their reliance on the training data. Notably, the performance
of our top ensemble model, which combines the predictions of all five networks,
equals that of a human expert with 0.8497 APM. This study sets a new standard for
the analysis of blood cells in microscopic images and opens up new possibilities
for the digital analysis of microbiological tests. This study's code and data are

Image acquisition processes in digital photography involve a range of color alterations due to the interaction of light with camera sensors and filters. These color alterations can significantly impact the final visual appearance of the photograph as well as the results of any subsequent retouching operations.  Historically, the majority of fluorescence emission spectra peak in the blue region of the visible spectrum.  Consequently, high-velocity decoloration processes, which are commonly used in photography, can amplify this phenomenon, yielding bright blue images.  A novel empirical approach has been developed to model this specific type of color alteration, which is centered on changes to the hue temperature of an image.  Unlike traditional high-velocity decoloration models that rely on chromaticity space, this new method is based on hue temperature and can be integrated into current rendering pipelines with relative ease.  Experimental results validate the proposed approach and highlight its practical applications in photography, including fluorescence effects and colorized X-rays, which are all exemplified through a range of striking photographic examples.  Moreover, the proposed methodology can be adapted to model a range of other fluorescence effects, which are supported by a wide variety of empirical evidence.  Notably, fluorescence effects, which are predicted by the proposed approach, have been observed in numerous medical imaging techniques including X-ray fluorescence imaging, photoacoustic imaging and bio-luminescent imaging.  These imaging techniques not only provide a wealth of empirical data to inform the proposed approach but also hold significant potential for a range of biomedical applications.  A general comparison between the proposed empirical model and existing high-velocity decoloration models reveals several key differences, which are supported by a range of empirical data.  Notably, the proposed approach is more in line with the fluorescence spectra of quinacrine in oil-based systems, which is consistent with its observed effects in oil-based systems that involve a range of high-velocity decoloration processes.  These findings highlight an important safety concern, which is that a portion of oil-based systems that have been treated with quinacrine may yield blue images that are incorrectly interpreted as being affected by high-velocity decoloration processes.  A detailed discussion of these potential misdiagnosis is provided in a companion document that is available online.  Notwithstanding these potential safety limitations, the proposed approach is expected to be highly useful in a range of applications and will likely have a significant impact on a range of fields including photography, fluorescence spectroscopy, X-ray fluorescence, photoacoustic imaging and fluorescence microscopy. This study presents an efficient method for converting relational data, represented by Shape Expressions, into RDF. The proposed solution is grounded in the principles of para-closure tables, allowing for the seamless adaptation of various data management systems, including those employing Shape Expressions, to support RDF data structure conversions. The effectiveness of the method was demonstrated through an experimental comparison of existing and proposed conversion techniques. The RDMQ-RDF algorithm was developed, building on existing concepts from Frohdi and para-closure tables, and was successfully implemented in a Java-based prototype. The prototype's performance was tested and evaluated in terms of its processing speed. The study's findings indicate that the proposed conversion approach is highly efficient and capable of handling large data sets quickly. A comprehensive evaluation was conducted to assess the accuracy and effectiveness of the method, revealing that it consistently yields accurate results and can effectively convert diverse data management systems to RDF. The study's outcomes have been applied to shape RDF data structures in order to facilitate their utilization in diverse contexts within resource management. The presented algorithm and its implementation have been made publicly available to inspire future research and facilitate practical applications. A StoNED boundary is the convex hull of a "noise envelope" resulting from various robust regression techniques, providing a tight estimate of the underlying regression boundary. The StoNED boundary boasts optimal robustness and strong theoretical guarantees. Classic examples of StoNED boundaries can be found in (Antic et al., 2018) [1] for Loftus-Rosenberg data and (Breunig et al., 1997) [19] for the Red Wine dataset. The pyStoNED Python package is now available to access a range of established and cutting-edge StoNED boundaries. This package includes support for: (a) the Red Wine and Loftus-Rosenberg datasets (b) generic Modelling of the noise envelope (c) the use of Gaussian Mixture Models to define the noise envelope (d) the application of kernel methods. pyStoNED also facilitates data generation, boundary visualisation, and comes with pre-installed data sets. Users can easily define custom noise envelopes and fit StoNED boundaries to new data. This package is distributed under the BSD-3 license and can be installed via pip: pip install pyStoNED. The source code can be found at https://github.com/valeriovanaretto/pyStoNED.

Leveraging the collective knowledge of the global community through open-source sharing of research and software has been instrumental in achieving this advancement. Presently, high-quality automated speech recognition solutions are available in a limited number of languages, primarily English. In contrast, languages with smaller user bases, including German, are often overlooked. This paper aims to address this gap by adapting a widely used, open-source speech recognition framework known as Swin-Transformer V5 from English to German. To optimize the process, a large, automatically generated dictionary and a high-quality German text for model fine-tuning are developed. This paper formulates the Faber-Krahn inequality for the Faber-Krahn inequality with a Robin boundary condition applied to the Hermite operator. Assuming a zero mean value on the boundary, the inequality is proven to take the form 

$\lambda_1(\mathcal{O},\beta) \ge \frac{c_N}{\mathrm{vol}(\mathcal{O})}$

for a positive constant $c_N$ and a unit ball volume $\mathrm{vol}(\mathcal{O})$. Moreover, the constant $c_N$ is dependent on $\beta$ and the dimension $N$ of the underlying space. Furthermore, the inequality becomes an equality when the ball is highly symmetric. This is achieved through introducing a positive solution to the eigenvalue equation for the Hermite operator with a Robin boundary condition, which is applied to a ball shape domain. Despite the widespread occurrence of non-Hermitian point-gap topography in driven quantum systems, it is often compromised by correlations between drivers and certain symmetries. This rule applies to a broad range of systems that experience periodically-driven quantum evolution, including optical lattices with coupled dimers and nonlinear resonators, where interactions between drivers lead to symmetry-based corrections that result in the cancellation of non-Hermitian point-gap topography. Our research reveals the underlying mechanism that causes this cancellation and demonstrates its practical implications by developing a driving protocol to restore the non-Hermitian point-gap topography in a correlated quantum system. This achievement enables the creation of a vast array of dynamic, interacting quantum states that are resistant to decoherence, including states that exhibit topological characteristics even when in contact with a bath of harmonic oscillators. Furthermore, our research showcases a novel approach to preserving the non-Hermitian point-gap topography in quantum systems through the use of engineered driver configurations. This method may have far-reaching implications for the theoretical understanding and practical development of topological quantum states that are resistant to decoherence and can be utilized in the construction of topological qubits. Moreover, our research may facilitate the development of topological states in systems that lack inherent symmetries, including systems consisting of coupled microcavities and atoms. Finally, our research may contribute to a deeper understanding of the interplay between non-Hermitian point-gap topography and correlations in the context of quantum phase transitions, including the possible restoration of non-Hermitian point-gap topography in systems that are in a critical state. Overall, our research from this study may lead to a significant advancement in the field of topological quantum mechanics and quantum information systems. Our research project aimed to develop characteristics of spoken language that reflect individual social traits. We, unlike previous studies, examined identity traits such as assertiveness and agreeableness through the tone, pace, and emotional content of spoken language, rather than just its emotional tone. To identify correlations between these traits and speech characteristics, we collected a vast dataset of spoken dialogue, which included ratings of speakers' assertiveness and agreeableness. We used statistical models to establish a relationship between speech characteristics and these ratings, allowing us to create a set of algorithms that modify synthetic speech to convey specific social traits. We tested the effectiveness of our algorithms by conducting a listening experiment and found that participants could accurately detect the intended traits in the modified synthetic speech. Furthermore, we discovered that our socially-aware modification techniques were more effective than a baseline method in replicating the full range of social traits in synthetic speech. The results of our study are a significant step towards creating more realistic and varied synthetic speech that reflects the speaker's unique social characteristics. The results of our study lay the groundwork for creating more sophisticated social speech synthesis systems that can accurately convey a wide range of emotions in synthetic speech. A new theoretical framework is suggested to address the issues of non-observed dark matter and flavour anomalies.  A group of standard model-like particles plus a set of vector-like fermions, vector-like scalars, and one scalar doublet is proposed, with the dark matter consisting of three colour-singlet luminous fermions.  A mechanism is introduced for the dark matter to auto-interact through the exchange of a $U(1)_{B-L}$ gauge boson, with additional auto-interactions facilitated by intermediate vector-like scalars.  Additionally, the presence of the $U(1)_{B-L}$ gauge symmetry itself serves as an auto-interaction mechanism.  A model of modular $A_4$ family symmetry is used to explain quark masses and the CP-violating kaon mass difference, as well as quark flavours.  Furthermore, the presence of both standard model and $U(1)_{B-L}$ Yukawa interactions allows for a natural explanation of the CP-violating kaon mass difference.  A matching analysis for the dark matter relic density and direct detection results confirms the feasibility of the suggested dark matter candidate.  The model also contains a natural solution for flavour anomalies, specifically in the mass of the $B$ meson.  A detailed discussion of the one-loop effective neutrino mass is conducted.  Lastly, the suggested model is testable via experiments searching for $W$-boson and $Z'$-boson production.  A detailed discussion of the suggested model's testability through experiments searching for $W$-boson and $Z'$-boson production is included. We develop a quasiparticle approximation based on the deformed Dirac equation to study the collective behavior of triaxial nuclei. Our results indicate that the minimal length parameter has a significant influence on the eigenvalues of collective motion, aligning with experimental data provided by $\gamma$-ray bands. We identify four degenerate states with the same energy for $\epsilon=0.05$, $\gamma \approx 60^\circ$, and $\beta \approx 0.6$. Introducing a hidden-variable framework based on simplicial complex topology provides a visual representation of the invariant set, enabling its description and analysis through geometric and topological tools. A novel hidden-variable framework has been established for the invariant-set hypothesis, focusing on the minimal topological structure required and enabling its use as a probabilistic model for quantum mechanics, the nontriviality of which is dependent on certain topological assumptions. Our work lays the ground for an in-depth examination of the nontriviality of the superdeterministic invariant-set hypothesis in a hidden-variable framework. Furthermore, a detailed description of the invariant set associated with the GHZ state on three qubits is constructed and analyzed, leveraging topology to gain insights into this fundamental quantum system. Our methods are universally applicable to higher qubit systems, extending far beyond the capabilities of topological data analysis, an emerging field widely utilized in modern mathematics. Moreover, our approach provides the means to computationally evaluate and compare the various topological structures underlying the invariant sets of different quantum systems, an ability that might lead to new breakthroughs in fundamental quantum information research. As an example of the utility of these topological structures, we computationally investigated the possibility of reducing non-trivial topological structures in certain quantum systems, a topic of ongoing debate in the literature. Our simulation reveals that the superdeterministic invariant-set hypothesis in a hidden-variable framework is compatible with this possibility, potentially resolving the related open question. Our simulation's precision is directly tied to the topological structure's properties; thus, any further insights or methods that refine our understanding of the topological structures underlying the invariant sets could significantly enhance the accuracy of the simulation. We explore various statistical mechanics models on a square lattice, considering systems with and without gauge fields. Focusing on models for two-dimensional fermions, we look at dimer configurations that can be either non-frustrated (with either no dimer overlaps or specific overlaps on specific pairs) or frustrated. Our goal is to identify the relationship between fermion dispersion relations and lattice structure. We first verify that non-frustrated dimer configurations match the expected dispersion relations for a non-disordered, two-dimensional Dirac fermion system. Next, we introduce a dimer overlap control parameter, $p$, on the lattice and compute corresponding gauge field and dimer configurations. We represent the results using a new, compact coordinate system tailored to each $p$. Our approach ensures that all important features of the fermion dispersion can be understood in this coordinate system. We analyze the fermion dispersion bands and bracketing for all values of $p$. Furthermore, we study how the gauge field and dimer configurations evolve with the dimer overlap parameter $p$, starting from the non-frustrated, non-overlapping dimer configuration ($p=0$) and an overcomplete, non-overlapping dimer configuration ($p=1$). We apply this understanding to develop a dimer configuration corresponding to the expected Dirac dispersion relations at $p=\infty$. Our work also has implications for the creation of novel topological materials. We apply our method in the construction of two-dimensional Dirac fermions with various properties such as (1) zero dissipation and mobility at the Dirac points; (2) a gap in the dispersion relations without breaking symmetry; (3) non-zero Hall conductivity in several different topological systems with various band structures. We also explore the possibility of achieving topological properties without breaking the electronic symmetry of the crystal or lattice structure by introducing orbital degeneracy. Our approach has been verified to have robust results by thorough checks. We have also created a visual illustration program using the Matplotlib library to facilitate the understanding of the dimer configurations and fermion dispersion relations, as provided in the supplementary materials. The work has been made public with the inclusion of numerous supplementary files such as the input and output files for the trivalent-plot program. For embedded real-time systems, a new, mixed-importance concept has emerged, requiring hybrid performance and reliability. Existing solutions fall short in addressing this need, as they either fail to provide performance guarantees or compromise reliability. A new approach, using hypervisor technology, is presented, demonstrating the capability to enhance embedded real-time system security through fault isolation. Furthermore, hypervisor-based virtualization is a proven technique that can utilize unexploited hardware virtualization resources to improve performance. This paper proposes the T-Visor, a commercial-grade hypervisor, designed for mixed-importance embedded real-time systems, achieving both reliability and performance through hypervisor-assisted fault detection, isolation, and mixed-importance scheduling. Experimental results show that T-Visor can efficiently detect and isolate faults while improving overall system performance. Compared to current hypervisor technologies, T-Visor is distinguished by its support for mixed-importance scheduling, delivering superior performance and reliability. This work is a significant contribution to the field of embedded real-time systems, offering a reliable and efficient solution for mixed-importance scheduling. A practical hypervisor implementation is provided, along with evaluation results, to demonstrate its effectiveness. The research has been validated by developing the T-Visor on QEMU and RISC-V platforms. In particular, the most critical fault detection and trade-off analysis are conducted in comparison to existing state-of-the-art (x86) hypervisors. This work is expected to inspire future research in embedded real-time systems and hypervisor-assisted fault detection and isolation. We analyze chimeras in networks where two equal subgroups are connected to a shared common pool, with each subgroup consisting of identical, uniformly heterogeneous nodes. Using a two-layer approach, we combine analytical and numerical methods to explore chimeras as oscillating and asynchronous states. When the coupling is weak, we observe chimeras that sustain oscillations and others that remain asynchronous. As network heterogeneity increases, a transition occurs from synchronous to asynchronous behavior. Notably, strong common signals can only penetrate and synchronize nodes within the homogeneous subgroup, leaving nodes in the heterogeneous group isolated and asynchronous. Furthermore, we find that chimeras are more common in networks with a large number of strong, high-frequency connections than in those with a large number of weak, low-frequency connections. Our findings are confirmed using numerical simulations of coupled phase oscillators and finite Markov model systems. Additionally, we expand our theoretical model to investigate chimeras in networks consisting of four equal subgroups and demonstrate that these phenomena are also relevant to biological systems, using the example of Drosophila melanogaster circadian rhythms in fruit flies. Automated controller design using model-based reinforcement learning has become a preferred method in various industries. However, developing controllers for complex systems that exhibit erratic behavior due to system failures or changes in their environment is particularly challenging. This problem is more formally identified as a Stochastic Markov Decision Process (MDP) since it involves making probabilistic calculations for the system's transition and reward functions. In response to this, researchers have proposed a novel, detailed approach for constructing robust Markov decision processes. This model-driven method integrates reinforcement learning with probabilistic controller design, ensuring resilience through model-driven criteria. The approach is demonstrated through its application in the anti-windup problem, where it successfully eliminates oscillations caused by controller saturation. Additionally, this method's adaptability is showcased through its application under uncertain and variable system conditions. The results of our experiments indicate a notable improvement in the robustness of our designed controllers when tested against typical model-based reinforcement learning approaches. Overall, this method offers a viable option for designing resilient, fail-safe controllers using the uncertainty models of system components. This research has far-reaching implications in various fields, including the design of quadcopters, power systems, and autonomous vehicles. The associated code for this research has been made publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/sameh-V/RWA_MBL. This resource includes our detailed modeling and design procedures. The detailed experimental findings, including the detailed numerical data and the generated controllers, can be accessed at https://doi.org/10.6084/M1.DA.YJMM.AT2N. The generated controllers can be directly implemented, whereas the detailed numerical data can be utilized for further research purposes. The purpose of these repositories is to promote the dissemination of research. The analysis reveals that the designed controllers exhibit an impressive 98% level of robust achievement, far surpassing the conventional model-based reinforcement learning methods which achieve only 35%. The underlying cause of this notable disparity is the critical role of failure probability in influencing dynamic system behavior, a relationship previously overlooked in most related literature. This critical insight has the potential to transform the design of multiple failure-prone systems, impacting a wide array of applications. The analysis of our experimental findings highlights the dynamic system's capacity to operate safely and efficiently in the presence of various model uncertainties, demonstrating the importance of incorporating failure probability in dynamic system modeling. The approach we present in this research bridges a significant knowledge gap by integrating reinforcement learning with the problem of designing resilient controllers, a task crucial for ensuring system safety and operation in the face of various failure

This concept is then developed to describe rings within a subcategory of $k$-dimensional objects in a 2-category, which are then called higher slice rings. By examining the commutative and graded structures within these rings, a diagramatic approach is introduced to study diagrams that consist of compositions of $k$-dimensional objects and their morphisms. This concept is particularly interesting in categories where dimensions intersect or combine in various ways. Several examples are given to demonstrate the significance of this idea in areas such as inclusions of sites, (higher) étale geometry, and the context of motivic twisted differential graded algebra. Furthermore, the framework of higher slice rings is used to systematize and expand the study of permutive diagrams, which have been studied in depth in a previous work, and also to explore the potential generalization of Gelfand-Kuznet's theory of permutive diagrams to the context of graded modules within graded rings. Lastly, the results and findings from the study of permutive diagrams are shown to be applicable in a more general context. This is based on the observation that any higher slice ring can be treated as a graded ring within a more extensive category, which is a combination of sites with dimensions greater than $k$. Several key concepts and results within Gelfand-Kuznet's theory are then derived in a more general context. In the realm of quantum gravity, random tensor networks serve as a suitable model for both compacted dimensions and quantum chaos.  In a recently published study, we explore the relationship between a key property, the entanglement entropy, and the angles of reflection within a chaotic tensor network.  Unlike its counterpart in one-dimensional systems, the entanglement entropy in higher dimensions is influenced by a multitude of reflection angles.  By examining the average and higher-order moments of the entanglement entropy, we pinpoint the underlying interplay between these parameters.  These statistical characteristics form the basis of refined entropy as a, proximal and nonperturbative, spectral indicator of eigenvalue eigenfunctions, capable of capturing intricate aspects of chaotic dynamics.  Moreover, we demonstrate that our method can be applied to a broad range of tensor networks, including randomly curved and gapped structures of holographic systems.  The effect of quantum gravitational dynamics on entanglement is thus fully characterized through the refined entropy.  Furthermore, the support of the entropy's distribution is found to be related to the collective behavior of eigenvalues.  Specifically, the expectation value of the entanglement entropy aligns with the Barbero-Immirzi parameter in holographic systems, while its higher-order moments exhibit a multifold increase in standard deviation with the number of reflection angles.  These outcomes align with the notion that chaos in quantum systems is linked to the breaking of time-dilation in quantum gravity, with angles of reflection serving as effective degrees of freedom.  The refinement of entropy provides valuable insights into the eigenvalue eigenfunctions of chaotic systems, revealing relationships between ergodic eigenstates and angles of reflection.  The application of refined entropy to holographic tensor networks allows us to extract information on ergodic patterns in systems possessing spatial structure, with the expectation value and variance of the entanglement entropy serving as metrics for ergodicity and spectral complexity.  The structure of eigenvalue eigenfunctions within a chaotic system is thus illuminated through the statistical properties of entanglement, which are influenced by reflection angles.  The refinement of entropy thus empowers the detection of ergodic patterns in quantum gravity and related systems, with potential applications to the study of quantum chaos and related phenomena. Patterns and structure that persist in space and time result from a combination of variability and organization. In this work, we delve into the fundamental principles of maintaining organization, focusing on how local interactions and hereditary information contribute to system stability. We introduce a concept from information theory, known as thermodynamic order, that quantifies the average amount of internal system organization. Our research demonstrates that spatial systems employing mean-field feedback mechanisms can increase their thermodynamic order by doing work without relying on external sources, as illustrated through a simple genetic model. Furthermore, we explore the general conditions under which self-organization is possible in non-equilibrium stochastic systems. These conditions are analogous to the requirements for self-organization in dissipative systems, as expressed by the autocatalytic cycle concept. We then discuss the limitations and potential applications of this theory. An analysis of a simplified model reveals that in most cases, pattern persistence is subject to these conditions, but there are instances where the principle does not apply as expected. These counterexamples highlight the significance of the system's dynamics and the nature of the organization involved. Ultimately, our research confirms that the interplay of hereditary information, feedback mechanisms, and stochastic dynamics provides a foundation for understanding and quantifying the emergence of spatial patterns and persistent organization. As a result, the concepts and theory introduced herein have far-reaching implications for our understanding of life, matter, and energy. They may also inspire advancements in engineering and artificial intelligence. We conclude by discussing future research opportunities at the interface of theoretical concepts and practical applications. The supporting materials can be found at the provided URL. A comprehensive review of our work was published in the book "Physics of Life: From Quantum Physics to Biology", as referenced. The essence of gravitational holonomy, a concept that encompasses both electromagnetic and gravitational force, was first introduced by Tresch, yet in a form that wasn't fully consistent with the principles of the U(1) gauge theory. The main objective of this paper is to build on Tresch's work, with the goal of deriving the gauge field equation in a four-dimensional flat space. The study starts with an intuitive explanation of Tresch's discovery, followed by the definition of gravitational holonomy. By utilizing techniques common to the gauge theory, it is demonstrated that the gravitational holonomy, when combined with the gauge transformation, adheres to the U(1) Abelian principle. Consequently, this revelation allows for the creation of gauge equation and strength tensor within the context of flat space. The study culminates with an exploration of gauge equation symmetry and the properties of gauge-invariant objects. It is discovered that gauge equation symmetry possesses three types of invariance: two that are directly linked to gauge transformations, and one that is associated with the time shift. We also verify that the strength tensor, a representation of gravitational holonomy, complies with gauge equation and reveal that it is the only consistent strength tensor. As a result, this study provides a U(1) Abelian framework for the gravitational gauge field and the gauge-invariant objects, the strength tensor and its field strength. Furthermore, this framework holds potential for the creation of consistent gravitational interactions among multiple gauge fields through the process of gauge accumulation. The study also opens up possibilities for the derivation of quantum gravitational equations using a generalized quantum formalism known as the quantum two-point function method. Consequently, this allows for the computation of systematic quantum corrections to gravitational interactions. We have intentionally omitted detailed derivation of gauge equation for gauge field and field strength in higher-dimensional spaces, leaving this for a future study. The study does however provide an opportunity for the creation of consistent higher-dimensional gravitational interactions between gauge fields and to the derivation of quantum corrections to gravitational interactions in four-dimensional and higher-dimensional spaces. We examine the set of Young diagrams with even or odd hook lengths that can be divided by 2 or 3. By establishing a connection between these diagrams and the modular properties of symmetric polynomials, we identify the generating functions for their hook lengths that are multiples of 2 or 3. These hook lengths' distributions are then used to calculate the fractions of Young configurations whose hook lengths can be divided by 2 or 3 in two or three ways. Finally, by leveraging computational capabilities, we simulate and plot the resulting hook length distributions in Young diagrams across a range of n from 6 to 24. The simulated results for n ≥ 8 accurately align with our analytical predictions. For n ≤ 7, minor discrepancies arise due to time constraints in the computational process. The precise error amounts are also determined. As a byproduct, we derive the total fractions of Young configurations with hook lengths that can be divided by 2, 3, or 6 in six distinct ways. Moreover, we obtain the asymptotic proportions for n → ∞. The accuracy of our analytical and computational findings for hook length distributions is substantiated through additional verification in the smallest n from 1 to 7. The supporting data for these results is presented graphically in a supplemental resource. The present study is part of a broader research initiative focused on the asymptotic properties of Young configurations with specific hook lengths, which are currently in development. The underlying methodology for these investigations will be outlined in a forthcoming publication. The experimental results demonstrate the NS model's capability to evolve a superior ensemble network with high predictive accuracy from the beginning of the learning process. Furthermore, the proposed method is scalable and can be effectively applied to real-world datasets, such as image and text domains. Given a generalized shape $K$, we establish a connection between its reference frames and a specific set of solutions to the Einstein vacuum equations with respect to $K$. This relationship serves as an extension to the well-documented correlation between Jacobi fields on a shape and metrics in four-dimensional general relativity. Notably, our work recovers key outcomes previously obtained by Stacey in the context of the Schwarzschild and Kasner metrics, while also providing an alternative explanation for the discovery of new Ricci-flat metrics constructed using shapes derived from left-invariant vector fields on certain Lie groups. These group shapes include geometric constructs such as hyperboloids, gyrotspheres and gyrocylinders. Our approach enables the generation of new solutions for the Einstein equations, as well as offers an intuitive understanding of existing solutions, was provided in Stacey's thesis. Furthermore, our solution-generating technique, which requires minimal computational effort, allows us to rapidly create numerous solutions for the Einstein equations by combining various products and quotients of shapes. This efficient method accommodates the formation of solutions regardless of their positive or negative scaling. As a demonstration of this process, we construct multiple new Ricci-flat metrics in four dimensions, including several known and currently undisclosed solutions. This extensive collection of solutions includes known solutions derived from products and quotients of the Schwarzschild and Kasner metrics, as well as two previously unpublished solutions obtained using G$_2$-gyrocylinders. Each of these discovered solutions is characterized by unique constants, expressions, and patterns. In addition to these findings, we also outline several promising research directions inspired by the new solutions, including the investigation of their properties and physics. Notably, these studies could potentially shed light on distinct phases observed in binary black hole mergers, a topic closely related to the study of gravitational wave properties in the LIGO and Virgo cosmology projects. As an example of this research direction, we offer an initial analysis of how the recently discovered solution generated using the $G_2$-gyrocylinder might describe a distinct self-gravitating spinning geodesic complete metric. This newly discovered solution is part of a subclass known as thePP$^3$-submanifolds class. Our analysis, in turn, contributes to the broader study of this particular subclass within the context of generalized shapes. In this research, we identify the exact formulas for calculating the counts of permutation functions and complete permutation functions within the finite field $\mathbb{F}_{q^{3}}$. Furthermore, we derive a formula for the tally of distinct permutation functions over the finite field $\mathbb{F}_{q^{n}}$ for any given $n$, providing a solution to an additional posed problem. The methods employed in this research involve constructing specific generating functions to tackle these counting problems. The derived formulas are then verified through coefficient comparison, utilizing combinatorial principles to establish relationships between polynomial coefficients. When working with cosmic microwave background (CMB) maps, it's essential to carry out data analysis in the vicinity of a point origin, but some techniques employed do not guarantee this condition known as "inversion symmetry." This concern necessitates the application of methods like maximum likelihood estimation that facilitate the realization of the symmetry. The process of achieving this symmetry can be cumbersome, but it's crucial for applications such as principle component analysis and estimation techniques. This article discusses a method for incorporating symmetry into the inversion symmetry-invariant maximum likelihood estimation process, specifically in the context of CMB estimation. The CMB symmetry is a crucial element in estimating quantities like the spectrum, thus it's necessary to ensure new estimation techniques and methods maintain this symmetry to avoid introducing anisotropic biases. The article provides specific examples related to CMB research, including how to incorporate symmetry into spherical deconvolution, estimation of angular auto-correlation power-spectra and non-Gaussian measures, and seismic inversion. The article also discusses an extension of the S4 estimator to ensure the CMB symmetry in practice. The extended S4 estimator, called S4inv, is based on a log-likelihood marginalization approach combined with inversion symmetry-invariant reconstruction techniques such as the S4 estimator and a symmetry-invariant deconvolution method for the isotropic part. The article also shows that CMB symmetry is a necessary condition for estimating quantities like E-mode bias, thus establishing a new direction of research. The article provides specific examples and practical advice on how to ensure this bias estimation condition, thus opening a new area of research. This treatment is incorporated into the policy's goal description, enabling it to learn multiple objectives simultaneously. Experimental results show that natural language descriptions can be effective for RL input, but also that the proposed method addresses the issue of ambiguity. Moreover, a comparison of different approaches to handling goals demonstrates that the proposed method significantly reduces the impact of ambiguity. This work is further illustrated by a study demonstrating a robot capable of following natural language instructions to perform unique tasks. This study showcases the importance of addressing referential ambiguity when applying reinforcement learning in real-world contexts. Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) are gaining attention as low-cost drones are increasingly available for a wide range of civilian purposes. The fourth generation of mobile networks (5G) is transforming UAVs into portable cells that can provide high-speed internet connections wherever needed. This study focuses on optimizing UAV routes to ensure that 5G-enabled drones can provide internet to IoT devices within a specified time frame while simultaneously achieving maximum speed in downloading uploaded data. The proposed solution involves dividing the problem into two distinct subtasks: (i) identifying the most suitable cell tower for each IoT device and (ii) designing the most efficient UAV route. This approach combines a greedy algorithm and a pre-computing method to solve the first subtask, while employing a flight route optimization method to solve the second one. The proposed solution is evaluated using an adapted version of the 5G-UAV scenario in a real-world city environment. The experimental results demonstrate that our solution can achieve a significant download speed improvement of 3.16 times compared to the existing benchmark speed of 5G-UAV. Furthermore, the results show that the optimized UAV route causes minimal geographical displacement, resulting in an average reduction of 25.69% in total distance compared to the shortest possible distance between UAV and IoT devices. The proposed solution has been successfully tested on local city maps of New York, Los Angeles, Chicago, San Francisco, Boston and Seattle. The structural relationship between the conformation of doped fullerenes and the surface interaction with supporting substrates has yet to be fully understood. By using scanning tunneling microscopy, the conformation of Sc2TbN@C80 on a (h-BN)/Ni(111) surface was studied at varying temperatures. It was observed that the particle undergoes a reversible shape transformation, shifting from a pentagonal-rich structure to a square-based configuration and back to the initial form, as the temperature changed. A theoretical model supports the experimental findings, indicating that the structural change occurs because the particle's reorganization involves both the carbon shell and the surface interaction with the (h-BN) layer, rather than simply adhering to the substrate. The set $\mathcal{C}$ is defined by specific conditions involving univalent functions from the real to the real domain. Chosen is the condition where the first derivative of such functions has a finite and positive absolute value for all x. This was done to facilitate a generalization and exploration of periodic planar dynamical systems with the aforementioned properties. A generalized form of the Birkhoff Alternative is investigated in this study. It is shown that SSMDTDD planar dynamical systems can exhibit any behavior within the following categories: (i) equilibrium, periodic, or rigorous irregular; (ii) or display either rough or smooth non-persistence with respect to certain small perturbations. Irrsolutability is defined as a system where none of its trajectories converge to an equilibrium point. A new classification of irregular behavior is also established. This study heavily relies on the application of Bautin multiplicators in the analysis and interpretation of the obtained results. A comprehensive study examining the dynamical behavior of smooth planar systems subject to small and small-to-large parameters is a significant outcome of this investigation. It is shown that most (80%) outcomes correspond to smooth non-persistence with corresponding rough or smooth ir-regularity outcomes accounting for the remainder. This study set the groundwork for investigating the dynamical behavior of discrete-time systems with smooth, strongly monotonic characteristics using codimension-two bifurcations. It is demonstrated that in such systems, the resulting behavior is widely determined (a typical case) and is often accompanied by various feature-rich outcomes, including irregularity, period doubling, multi-cycles, and chaos. A theoretical model based on the one-dimensional logistic map is used in this investigation. This model predicts the occurrence of six distinct patterns of irregular behavior, including rough (asymptotically stable ir-rational set), semi-irregular (asymptotically stable ir-rational set with semi-local exponential stability), period doubling, multi-cycles, chaotic (transitive set with semi-local exponential transitivity), and chaotic-like scenarios. These patterns correspond to different ir-rational set stability conditions. This study also explores the relationships between corresponding features observed in discrete-time systems with smooth, strongly monotonic characteristics and their corresponding smooth, strongly monotonic planar systems. The potential of using noisy intermediate-scale quantum computers with the variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) lies in molecular simulations, where accurately constructing an ansatz using a shallow quantum circuit is key to successful implementation. Instead of meticulously designing the ansatz, we suggest learning its parameters automatically through an adaptive VQE method that utilizes qubit excitations to improve convergence. By iteratively adding excitation operators to flawed ansatz layers, the adaptiveVQE method effectively tackles ansatz errors and enhances overall performance. Experimental results using both simulated and real quantum processors demonstrate that the adaptiveVQE method outperforms standard VQE, especially in challenging cases where the target ground state has a high excitation error rate. With its use of qubit excitations, the adaptiveVQE method offers a well-defined quantum chemistry framework that addresses issues related to multi-qubit entanglement. Its ability to successfully simulate the helium and lithium dioxide molecules makes the adaptiveVQE method a promising approach for future quantum chemistry applications. Furthermore, the method's ability to correctly calculate the spectroscopic constant for the neodymium ion in its doublet state, as well as accurately reproduce previous findings on the lithium molecule, highlights its potential for successful implementation with noisy intermediate-scale quantum computers. Finally, the adaptiveVQE method's ability to correctly calculate the neodymium ion's electronic transition energies, which are in line with existing knowledge, underscores its potential for successful use in a wide range of quantum chemistry applications. Moreover, the method's ability to correctly calculate the valence frequencies for $^{13}$C-ethylene and the neodymium ion's zero-phonon line, which agree with existing data, demonstrates its ability to successfully address issues related to quantum computing. An added benefit of its use of qubit excitations is the reduction of computational noise. A crucial element in many learning approaches is the transformative connection, which can have far-reaching consequences if not carefully managed. In particular, the risk of representation leakage in generative models poses a significant concern, as malicious entities can obtain valuable information about sensitive topics, such as individuals' faces or passwords, by manipulating the input to the generative model. As an effective technique to prevent this issue in the latent variable model, we developed the profound generative decoder (PGD), a method that uses maximum apportionment of representation to essentially eliminate the transformative connection. This method was inspired by the security method used in password storage, saltification. We show that the PGD is able to effectively prevent inference of private topics, keep the likelihood of representation manipulation low, and integrate easily with existing generative model frameworks. We also propose a method of utility measurement to evaluate trade-offs between the likelihood of generated data and the security of the model. We conducted a series of experiments to demonstrate the effectiveness of the PGD method on various generative models and datasets. These results show that the PGD can be used to significantly improve the security of existing generative models. For example, in the case of the Metropolis-Hastings algorithm, we found that the PGD can improve the security of the model by nearly an order of magnitude. The results of these experiments confirm the practicality and effectiveness of the PGD method. This work was previously known as arXiv's 2041.10515 poster. Our analysis of cosmic microwave background observations from Planck indicates subtle inaccuracies in the standard model of cosmic development. Furthermore, these discrepancies coincide with disagreements between the measurements of the Hubble constant made by the Baryon Acoustic Oscillations and the NANOGrav precursor experiments, which detected faint signs of gravitational waves. To address these issues, we suggest a concept in which inflation-produced gravitational waves are amplified by extra dimensions, leading to either a detection in NANOGrav's frequency range or a substantial boost in amplitude. Depending on the scenario with the most optimal parameters, we discover that these gravitational waves could cause discrepancies up to 1.7 standard deviations in the precision cosmology based on the Planck data, while also potentially resolving NANOGrav's results and reducing the discrepancy between the cosmic microwave background and the Hubble constant measurements to 1.5 standard deviations. Combining our findings with future data from the CMB, the TESS satellite, the LSST, and the Virgo/LIGO detector consortium may possibly confirm this theory. Conversely, if this theory is proven false, enhancing the precision of the Planck data and including other astrophysical observations might help in resolving the existing discrepancies in the standard model of cosmic development. The innovative framework of aspect-based sentiment analysis pinpointed the aspects of products or services contributing to people's opinions, but previous methods relied heavily on using training data with labeled sentiment labels. This requirement created an impractical scenario where comprehensive product reviews might need modified to include explicit sentiment phrases, directly opposing the purpose of using reviews for guidance. Additionally, most existing approaches fail to account for the reviews' implicit context. To tackle this challenge, we present a new supervised pre-training method that combines a newly proposed contrastive loss and a BERT-based framework. This method effectively utilizes explicit and implicit sentiment words to understand the opinions on specific product aspects, using linear transformation to integrate sentiment words' meaning into unique contrastive spaces. We test our approach's effectiveness on two prominent datasets and achieve the best results compared to other state-of-the-art methods. Current machine learning conventions recognize that training data can be flawed, biased, or incomplete, potentially harming model performance. To address these issues, our research delves into the concept of selectively ignoring or reevaluating data points. We focus on two core challenges: (1) determining which training data to discard and (2) improving existing labels by reviewing errors. To tackle these problems, we propose a framework grounded in the idea of ascribing credit or value to specific attributes of past experiences. This framework generates scenarios where target skills or concepts are evaluated with hindsight, emphasizing what was crucial for successful outcomes or feedback. By comparing past experiences against future similar scenarios, our method identifies relevant features that contributed to positive outcomes, effectively identifying suboptimal data points to discard and faulty labels to correct through self-correcting mechanisms. Our approach offers a flexible method for automatically reinterpreting training data, and we demonstrate its effectiveness in enhancing the performance of neural networks on challenging datasets by selectively omitting data points and modifying erroneous labels to improve model performance. The method is available online at a dedicated website. Moreover, our proposed technique extends to other methods, enabling self-improvement in a wide array of existing algorithms. A subsequent study explores the additional capabilities of this method. The groundings of our approach in a dynamic theory of learning are outlined in a companion paper. This paper introduces the Multilingual Event Extraction dataset, a groundbreaking resource for researching event extraction in multiple languages. This unique dataset is built on a set of specific topics, where each topic consists of events characterized by different semantic meanings. In contrast to most existing datasets, which typically feature single-word target events like "election" or "innovation", our dataset focuses on more complex multiple-word target events such as "terrorist attack" or "environmental innovation". Furthermore, our dataset differs from other multilingual datasets like XE and GIZELLE, which feature event names as the primary context, in that we have crafted detailed paragraph-level context for each event, aiming to enhance the difficulty of research models. To facilitate a challenging comparison, we have developed baseline models, as well as collected and made public the corresponding data, an industry-first in this field. This MEE dataset is designed to not only assess research models' ability to process multiple words but also their capacity to distinguish between events with intricate semantic connections. With a total of nearly 50,000 annotated sentences spanning three languages - English, Chinese, and Japanese - our dataset is set to become a leading benchmark for multilingual event extraction and discovery. Several approaches can be taken to model, improve, and analyze complex laser systems.  These methods leverage powerful computational tools and rely on detailed, accurate descriptions of the individual optical and mechanical components that make up these systems.  By integrating proprietary manufacturer supplied code with widely available tools such as ZEMAX and LASERMAX, it becomes possible to effectively design, model and refine complex laser systems.  Additionally, a previously developed method allows for a systematic backward-looking approach to analyze and troubleshoot malfunctioning laser systems.  In this presentation, these strategies will be discussed, including a detailed examination of the role of beam parameters and their impact on system design, along with a detailed explanation of the LASERMAX tool and its application.  Furthermore, examples illustrating the application of the reverse engineering method to analyze and troubleshoot malfunctioning high-power laser systems will be provided.  Finally, key findings from a recent application of the reverse engineering method to a commercial high-energy petawatt amplifier will be shared, including a detailed discussion of the importance of understanding system thermodynamics and the impact of the quantum noise limited noise source in high-energy systems.  These findings, along with recommendations for improving high-energy amplifier performance, will be presented.  It's worth noting that the analysis reveals that the high-energy system under examination failed to meet its energy output target, a common issue in high-energy systems.  A critical review of the system design, including an assessment of the active and passive components, as well as the laser beam delivery system, will be conducted to identify the root cause of the performance shortfall.  Through this in-depth analysis, the reasons for the system's suboptimal performance became clear and a plan to rectify the issue was developed.  These examples illustrate the value of accurate modeling, in-depth analysis, and thorough understanding of system thermodynamics and noise sources in high-energy systems.  The presentation will provide a comprehensive overview of these concepts and serve as a resource for designers, engineers, and scientists working to develop high-power, high-energy laser systems.  The presentation will conclude with a detailed discussion of future areas of improvement for high-energy systems, including areas that may contribute to reduced performance and serve as opportunities for future enhancement.  The presentation is intended to equip the audience with the knowledge and insights needed to design, improve, and analyze complex high-power and high-energy laser systems, as well as identify potential areas for future advancement. A cutting-edge approach for incorporating external images into text generation models involves adding image descriptors as hidden inputs. Current text generation models are typically trained in the absence of direct image information, stored somewhere within the model. Recent research using neural editors addresses this discrepancy but leaves the image information in a 'black box'. In this study, we explore a new method to integrate text and image domains by treating text generation as an image-guided process. We propose an image-based control descriptor system to facilitate this process, thereby allowing text generation models to utilize image information without relying on hidden inputs. Instead, we train convolutional neural networks to extract essential image characteristics, condense them into control features, and use them to fine-tune language models at the character level. Experiment results on two datasets demonstrate the efficacy of our approach, while a comparison with a related neural editor is also conducted. Further analysis reveals desirable image-guided text properties, and successfully apply the method to generate novel words. Moreover, our approach achieves consistent results across multiple image-guided text applications, opening new avenues for research and development. We also release our code and pre-trained models for public use. \medskip Our contribution can be summarized as: (i) introducing an image-based control system to condense and transmit image information into text generation models, (ii) proposing an innovative method to extract essential image characteristics, (iii) developing a character-level generation system to effectively utilize image guides, and (iv) successfully applying the method to various image and text domain integration tasks. (The work was first published in 2021; a revised version was released in 2022 with additional content and a more explicit conclusion section.) We introduce an upgraded RingCT protocol that supports stealth addresses in conjunction with Delegated Proof of Stake, resulting in Delegated RingCT.
The Delegated RingCT scheme is comprised of an integrated signature and encryption framework, combining a public key encryption protocol and two types of signatures along with linkable ring signatures, in order to facilitate transaction data encryption and non-transferable tokens usage within the same transaction.
Our research is focused on evaluating Delegated RingCT in comparison to the standard RingCT implementation within Bitcoin Silver, indicating that Delegated RingCT exhibits superior anonymity and throughput while reducing latency by 56%, when compared to RingCT.
The Delegated RingCT implementation also reveals an unanticipated finding, showing that Delegated RingCT takes less time to process than RingCT during regular network conditions, while also requiring smaller block sizes.
These outcomes demonstrate that Delegated RingCT can efficiently support RingCT-level anonymity while enhancing performance through increased throughput and decreased latency. 
As a result, Delegated RingCT presents a viable option for other cryptocurrencies looking to integrate similar anonymity systems. 
In summary, our research confirms Delegated RingCT as a faster and more secure anonymity solution. 
The Delegated RingCT codebase can be accessed at https://github.com/BitcoinSilver/BITSilver-groth17-ringct. 
This research benefits Bitcoin Silver and other RingCT-based cryptocurrencies, while also providing a foundation to develop future improvements in anonymity-preserving cryptocurrencies.

Building trusted models through collaborative effort requires careful data sharing and use among various parties, a process that must be both regulated and recorded for accountability and measurement.  Existing methods for collaborative modeling involve sharing pre-trained models and data, but neither fully convey the source dependence of such results.  In this work, we investigate the application of Bayesian learning and neural networks, combined with tools like IMIT, an open function library, to develop and share reliable uncertainty quantification for the results obtained.  We demonstrate the utility of this approach through a series of benchmark tests, evaluate its performance in real-world settings with a US government climate model and a NASA deep learning application, and recommend creation of an 'open metadata' standard to facilitate the sharing of collaborative modeling knowledge.  Our work identifies potential obstacles and benefits to sharing data and results, and we discuss the future developments and extensions expected to result from this effort.  Furthermore, we outline ways to expand neural network training at the agency level, including the use of Adversarial training, and expect this initiative to lead to significant advancements in the open source modeling domain.  The code used in this research is freely accessible through the commit repository.  Our work also contributes to the development of a new paradigm for collaborative data analysis and research, one that is characterized by a spirit of open and reciprocal cooperation.  We hope that our results will inspire other agencies and institutions to join us in this effort and to contribute their own results, data, and experience.  We anticipate a future where agencies can draw on a shared, ever-growing body of knowledge and data, and where researchers and analysts can work together in a spirit of mutual support and cooperation.
