Efficient neural network inference with low bandwidth and low processing cost quantized neural networks (QNNs) has become highly sought after. One popular approach, quantization neural networks (QuantNNs), restricts the weights and activations to low-bit binary values, significantly reducing bandwidth and processing requirements. However, this approach introduces significant accuracy loss as optimal thresholds and binary representations vary across layers and training phases. Current state-of-the-art techniques, such as DPX, approximate the optimal binary threshold for each weight through a continuous value, while utilizing discrete steps to search for optimal binary representations during the quantized training process. Although these techniques, though highly effective, face a trade-off between search efficiency and training time, due to the high time complexity involved. Our proposed an Anneewed Search technique, AskewSGD, addresses this trade-off by incorporating interval limited optimization (ILO) and maximally marginally nearest classifier (MMNC) to efficiently explore the discrete space of binary representations and identify the most suitable options for each layer and training phase. As a result, our AskewSGD method outperforms the current state-of-the-art approach, DPX, across a range of 0.2-1.3% in terms of accuracy, and 60% in terms of training speed. In recent years, biologically soft robotics has experienced rapid growth. This field is characterized by the absence of rigid components, allowing robots to achieve enhanced mobility and manipulate objects with greater precision. As a result, algorithms and techniques inspired by classical robot control have been adapted for application to soft robots. However, the inherent complexity of soft robotic systems, combined with their variability and non-linearity, poses significant automation challenges. To address these issues, experts from multiple fields, including engineering, physics, and mathematics, have developed models to analyze and simplify the behavior of these intricate systems. Model-driven control emerges as a promising approach, relying on advanced models to control soft robots effectively. This paper aims to provide an in-depth review of the model-driven control techniques recently developed for various types of soft robots. Additionally, the paper will examine the most effective control strategies and highlight the principal methodologies employed to design the controllers, focusing on the crucial role of modeling. Furthermore, the paper will identify the principal obstacles to introducing model-driven control in robotics and propose future directions for the research community. [Abstract] 

Although considerable progress has been made in recent years, soft robotics still faces numerous hurdles to realization. This review seeks to bridge the gap between robotics and control engineering communities, emphasizing the importance of modeling for model-driven control and presenting practical solutions to open issues. In addition, the review explores the use of computational methods in model-driven control and provides a comprehensive overview of the current state of the art as well as future research directions for the robotics community. [Abstract] 

This review begins by introducing the conceptual framework of model-driven control and its components. Next, it delves into the main characteristics of soft robotic systems and the essential features of models used in model-driven control. Following this, it presents the different types of models employed in model-driven control and reviews the prevalent control design methods used in model-driven control. Ultimately, it identifies the main obstacles to implementing model-driven control in soft robotics and proposes potential future research pathways. [Abstract] 

One of the principal hurdles to adopting model-driven control in soft robotics is developing high-quality models that meet the needs of this field. As a result, experts from multiple fields, including mechanics, physics, and mathematics, must work together to create reliable models of soft robotic systems. This requires collaboration and a shared understanding of the challenges and limitations of model-driven control in soft robotics. This review aims to spark interest in model-driven control and inspire breakthroughs in addressing the main obstacles to implementing model-driven control in soft robotics. [Abstract]

In conversational AI, interactions centered around verifying factual information play a vital role. A key feature of these interactions is the use of structured data, specifically tables, which contain multiple related facts. Current approaches focusing on language models, such as GPT-3, have proven effective in confirming individual facts extracted from these tables.  Despite their success, existing models fail to effectively utilize the structure and relationships within these tables to enhance fact confirmation.  In an effort to address these limitations, researchers have introduced the Table-oriented Fact Confirmation (TFC) task and proposed a modular decomposition approach for understanding the relationships within these tables.  This innovative method is comprised of two modules: a Relational Module and a Configular Module, which leverage different reasoning strategies to confirm facts in table-based settings.  Experimental results demonstrate that by combining these two modules, a linear model can surpass GPT-3's performance on the TFC task.  Moreover, analysis reveals that key factors, such as model size and hyperparameters, greatly influence TFC accuracy.  Future research could explore the potential of large language models, such as GPT-3, in learning this decomposition strategy and other strategies to improve TFC performance.

In distance labeling for planar graphs, each vertex is assigned a set of symbols that represents the minimum possible distance to other vertices. A problem proposed by Cielinski and Kowalczyk considered improving this concept by taking into account the effectiveness of identifying errors. To achieve this, an essential step is to be able to identify incorrect labels when a vertex's true neighbor is affected by a single error. Building upon an earlier method by Gaury et al that introduced a concept known as fault-tolerant distance labeling, our work presents an innovative scheme which combines efficiency and error tolerance by utilizing a specific type of distance labeling called rank-labeling in planar graphs. This novel scheme allows for the transmission of reduced data - only half the amount of symbols as there are vertices. Furthermore, our method ensures that a substantial portion of all possible errors can be identified, specifically at least a 25% increase in error detection over previous work. To validate our approach, a comprehensive study was conducted on various types of planar networks, revealing that our method adaptively adjusts its label size based on the structure of the graph, resulting in optimal labels of size O(V). Our experiments also show that our method is versatile and can be applied to a range of real-world networks. Interestingly, our method is found to be closely related to the solution of Gaury and Kowalczyk for the smallest possible fault-intolerant rank labels. Our test findings suggest that our method outperforms existing methods in several aspects, and result summaries are presented in a user-friendly format utilizing Tables and plots. The proposed method is implemented in a publicly accessible repository that includes sample network data for comparison purposes. Analysis of our results reveals that our approach provides a highly efficient and adaptable solution to the problem, and resulting labels can be viewed online. Recent studies demonstrate that models trained on broken datasets, particularly those with inconsistent or random outputs, exhibit characteristic patterns not found in normal data distributions. This phenomenon underpins the use of pattern-based methods for out-of-distribution detection, which have achieved notable success. However, existing approaches only consider mean and variance patterns and overlook other distribution characteristics. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel method called DNPL, built around a normal process with distributional layers. By representing an NP as a sequence of distributional layers, each capturing a distinct distribution characteristic (skewness, kurtosis, mode ambiguity, and tail anomalies), we develop an efficient model that effectively identifies anomalies both in classification and language tasks with improved accuracy and robustness. The introduced approach also enhances calibration, a desirable property in out-of-distribution detection. The proposed method's simplicity, efficacy, and theoretical grounding make DNPL a reliable out-of-distribution detection framework. The associated code can be found at https://github.com/andreabiscaldi/dnpl. Furthermore, our research reveals that models trained on broken datasets exhibit distinctive patterns in their distributional characteristics, which can be used to accurately identify out-of-distribution samples. This understanding has the potential to significantly improve ood detection methods by utilizing multiple distribution characteristics. Experimental results demonstrate that DNPL achieves high accuracy (99.96% on Clef 2020, 85.44% on ImageNet, and 99.58% on RobustBench) while also demonstrating instances of ood patterns, paving the way for generalization of the DNPL approach to various distribution characteristics and tasks. There is an increasing need to develop a timing model that accurately integrates the complex characteristics of modern optical clocks. Traditionally, optical clocks have been described using a Fourier-based repetition frequency model, but this model is inadequate in capturing the inherent features of state-of-the-art clocks. In contrast, our work presents a novel probabilistic timing model that considers the unique characteristics and fluctuations of advanced optical clocks operating at high precision levels, without assuming a repetitive structure. This model utilizes a Gaussian distribution to characterize the stochastic clock signal and introduces the concept of "timing events" to quantify the occurrence of clock phases. By deriving probability distributions for these events, the proposed model provides a comprehensive understanding of optical clock behavior in terms of clock cycles and fluctuations. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this probabilistic approach by applying it to simulations representing two distinct optical clock configurations. The development of this probabilistic model is particularly suited for use in high-precision optical clock applications, such as time dilation measurements and network synchronization. By dissecting the stochastic characteristics of optical clocks, this theory provides valuable insights for enhancing clock design and data analysis methods. In particular, this model is anticipated to find practical value in forthcoming research on time dilation using optical clocks with clocks operating on an atom beam. It is anticipated to facilitate a groundbreaking measurement with potential to shed new light on general relativity. Furthermore, this study is expected to pave the way for integrating optical clocks into large-scale scientific endeavors such as gravitational wave research. The model presented in this study is expected to facilitate significant advancements in the physics of gravity with precision exceeding that of the last decade's advancements. In addition to the theoretical aspects a comprehensive analysis of uncertainty is also presented with the application of the limit theorem for weakly dependent random variables along with the use of an integral transform for dependent random variables following a specific structure described in the paper. The proposed transformation has a, a priori, universal character and can be applied to any random variables when a method to quantify their dependence is known. As a demonstration of its capabilities this approach is applied to analyze data composed of a diverse range of random variables. The measurement of the dispersion relation's hydrodynamic branch by Pellegrino et al. and an analysis of daily precipitation data in Paris are two examples of its effectiveness. The proposed model is expected to facilitate similar research and measurements with precision optical clocks operating at high precision levels. The development of this model is expected to enhance our understanding of optical clock behavior in terms of clock cycles and fluctuations, a crucial step towards the development of precision optical clocks operating on an atom beam

Recent advancements in task-oriented metric learning have led to the creation of several distinct loss functions, typically implemented within small-scale classification systems, despite the lack of clear guidance on evaluating their performance in complex learning scenarios. To address this, we've developed a method called gradient surgery, allowing us to modify the output of already-trained neural networks by altering the distribution of class-specific gradients. This approach enables a more detailed analysis of the effects previously thought to be unique to specific loss functions on larger-scale classification tasks, and reveals that benefits associated with certain loss functions in smaller-scale systems are not universal. This empirical finding underscores the significance of methodologically driven experiments when exploring novel learning methods. Furthermore, we demonstrate that gradient surgery can be applied to investigate the influence of particular training data properties, and showcase its potential to create synthetic datasets with diminished diversity, thereby facilitating the production of high-quality models for difficult-to-simulate classification tasks. Finally, we outline potential future research directions based on our observations. The underlying code for this study can be accessed at https://github.com/alexkych/. In multi-armed bandit problems with time-varying payoffs, each arm has its own 
sequence of expected outcomes. We examine cases where the expected values depend 
on the arms themselves as well as the expected wait times for receiving outcomes, 
known as two-armed bandits with specialization. We investigate how these factors 
affect the performance of well-established upper confidence bound policies. For 
two-armed bandits with time-based payoffs and no specialization, it has been found 
that using a logarithmic number of samples is sufficient for an optimal upper limit 
in a given number of steps. We demonstrate in this study that a similar result does 
not hold true for two-armed bandits with specialization, instead illustrating that 
using a logarithmic number of samples may not be sufficient even if there is no 
correlation in the expected outcomes. An upper limit approach is proposed in this 
study that utilizes the expected wait times for making decisions, and it is found 
that using a logarithmic number of samples is sufficient for achieving an optimal 
upper limit in a given number of steps even in the case of two-armed bandits with 
arm-dependent wait times. We extend our approach to cover the case of multiple 
arms with various decision boundary conditions, and an empirical analysis is 
also presented in the study. An additional analysis is provided in an appendix 
to show that an approach based on the expected value and its standard deviation 
for determining the bound for each arm, yields comparable results that are within 
a logarithmic factor of the approach proposed in this study. We also present an 
empirical result in an appendix that an approach based on the expected value and 
its standard deviation performs within a factor of $O(\log\log k)/\tau$ of the 
optimal result for cases where the expected payoff function is non-decreasing. 
Furthermore, an approach is proposed in an appendix for finding a lower bound 
for the expected payoff function. An empirical analysis presented in the study 
suggests that an approach based on the expected value and its standard deviation

We propose the LEATHER framework, a modular structure that enables controlled
combinations of probabilistic dialogue models to develop coherent and natural
dialogue responses. This approach prioritizes understanding the underlying
logical (inference) and planning mechanisms in human conversation, which are
more prevalent than typical statistical associations in dialogue. By emulating
these cognitive processes, LEATHER yields flexible and extensible output,
allowing for various stylistic and linguistic adjustments. We incorporate
multiple learning strategies within the framework to account for distinct
aspects of dialogue, such as inference and planning. Empirically, LEATHER's
capacity to generate human-like dialogue is demonstrated through generated
utterances, both in-plane and off-plane. Furthermore, our research reveals a
connection between the various components within LEATHER and existing AI
technologies, highlighting that many current approaches to controlled dialogue
generation are inherently flawed. Finally, we outline the underlying
mechanisms driving natural human conversation and illustrate their relevance to
LEATHER's performance. The project's source code can be found at
https://github.com/philipnaccarato/LEATHER. This research received funding from
the Gatsby Charitable Foundation. The foundation's involvement is detailed in
Appendix C. The LEATHER project was previously described in Naccarato et al.
(2020) at the IJCAI-2020 conference. The current work presents significant
methodological improvements, leading to improved generative coherence and
inferences compared to the initial output. The updated LEATHER model was
previously released but lacked the underlying explanations, although the current
work fills this gap. The current work also addresses off-plane inferences and
integrates various stylistic factors to boost coherence and naturalness. The
source code for this work, as well as the models and data, can be found at
https://github.com/philipnaccarato/LEATHER-IJCAI2020-upgrade. The related
Gatsby Foundation report can be found at https://www.gatsby.org/emotional-wellbeing. In this review, the basic principles of lattice QCD and its computational methods are discussed, followed by illustrations of its applications in studying heavy atomic nuclei and the quark-gluon plasma in high-energy collisions. Furthermore, the review outlines ongoing challenges and future research directions in this field. Due to the volume's formatting constraints, the review primarily focuses on density rather than introducing the subject entirely from first principles. Additionally, the review primarily covers results and introduces theoretical foundations where necessary. The fundamental ideas behind lattice QCD and its underlying principles are described in detail. The review is divided into three sections, covering the underlying theory, numerical implementation, and eigenvalue distributions, especially in three-dimensional color SU(3) gauge theories on a lattice. The review then switches to discussing the reliance of lattice QCD on random matrix theory and eigenvalue computations. The latter section explores generalizations of lattice QCD, focusing on theories described using gauge-fixing methods in four-dimensional spacetime while adding complex components to the gluon field. The review concludes by outlining the role of density in these generalized lattice QCD models and their potential applications in studying the properties of atomic nuclei and quark-gluon plasma. The underlying lattice QCD methods are discussed in detail, and I explore concepts such as chiral symmetry, the Dirac operator, and the dependence of lattice models on the cutoff, especially in complex generalizations. The review then delves into the Monte Carlo sampling methods used in these generalized lattice QCD models and discusses the performance of fast and parallel algorithms on modern computing systems. The latter section explores generalizations of lattice QCD that incorporate interactions between gluons and fermions while adding complex components to the gluon and fermion fields. The review concludes by outlining the current state of lattice QCD research in this context and discussing the importance of quark masses, isospin asymmetry, and density in the theory. A specific machine-learning approach is formulated as a sequence of Gaussian Process predictions, targeted at simulating the dynamic forces acting on an offshore wind turbine. This sequential model, known as the Chained Gaussian Process (CGP), effectively computes the stress and strain induced in the turbine's hub as a result of wind, wave, and wind-wave interactions. Trainined using observational data from the IEA's 5-MW deepwater offshore wind test site, the CGP accurately models a range of turbulence-related characteristics essential for calculating turbine loads. Moreover, the method enables quick computation of the uncertainty associated with these loadings, making risk assessments for offshore wind turbines more informed and data-efficient. Utilizing the CGP, researchers were able to derive closed-form formulas for estimating the turbulence-related loads in significant offshore wind turbine components, including the blades and hub. These load calculations can be used to develop more reliable and robust wind-turbine design optimization strategies that incorporate uncertainty quantification, thereby maximizing energy production while minimizing operational risks. Several potential applications and future research directions are briefly outlined in the conclusion. The numerical code and data used in this study are publicly available on the OpenSource repository located at https://github.com/Caltech-CSE-Stat-Within-A-Week/2023-06-chained-gaussian-process. Further development and maintenance of this repository can be monitored at https://github.com/Caltech-CSE-Stat-Within-A-Week/Chained-Gaussian-Process/offshore-wind/tensor-and-sequential-gp. Additionally, the offshore wind turbine loads community can partake in the development of a novel tensor-based Gaussian Process framework as described at https://arxiv.org/doi/10.26411/2023.07311. We welcome collaboration and participation in the future development of these resources. The CGP model itself is currently being developed further at https://arxiv.org/doi/10.26411/2023.05796. Social media platforms serve as vital sources of data during natural disaster events, offering valuable information that can aid emergency response operations. Utilizing real-time analytics on social media content enables authorities to swiftly assess damage, monitor evacuation processes, and detect trending topics related to disaster updates. This study aims to illustrate the efficacy of social media analytics by investigating the Izmir earthquake in Turkey, where we performed a comprehensive analysis on Twitter data. Our work encompasses both qualitative and quantitative approaches to examine the earthquake's impact by examining damage and emotional levels on Twitter. Furthermore, we developed an interactive dashboard using Shiny for R, providing an accessible platform for researchers to analyze and explore social media data in real-time. This study can function as a foundation for future investigations on social media analytics in the context of disaster events. The associated data and code can be found at https://github.com/yasevmain/Izmir-Earthquake. The application can be accessed directly at https://izmir-earthquake-app.app.

For discrete groups G having a finite number of generators and isomorphic to an infinite nilpotent group, we determine R_\infty(G) for the general form of a quotient of the generalized solvable Baumslag-Solitar group, specifically BS(m,n) with m having a value of 1. If G is a group with a finite number of generators and isomorphic to a nilpotent group, it must have a non-trivial nilpotent quotient. In the case of a BS(m,n) group with m equal to 1, its nilpotent quotients are isomorphic to BS(n,c) with c having a value of 1. We will demonstrate that R_\infty(BS(n,c)) is equal to 1 plus 1/(n-1) times the sum of 1/(n-1) and 1, but this is under the condition where n and c are both greater than 1. In cases where either n or c has a value of 1, the group in question is isomorphic to either the free abelian group on two generators or the integer ring. We will also provide the solution to the problem of finding R_\infty for these two groups, which in turn will allow us to fully address Problem 1.16 in the book 'Geometric Group Theory' written by E. Shalom. We will prove that R_\infty for the group FreeZ(n) with n being two or more is equal to one. Recently, autonomous vehicles have gained significant interest due to their
potential to improve road safety and convenience. However, safely navigating
various driving environments remains a top challenge for several technical
barriers. Collecting extensive data from experienced drivers or automatic
agents is essential to overcome these limitations. This research introduces a
novel dataset called SceNDD, a large, unlabeled record of driving situations
captured through naturalistic observations. The associated labeling system relies
on a structured scenario, which involves dividing the g-spatial area into three
sections: proximity, surrounding, and background areas. The resulting labeling was
done manually, and the dataset includes various situations such as driving in
the city, intersections, or various weather conditions, totaling over 80,000
distinct scenarios. Our study shows that a self-attention-based model with a
simple transformer architecture can predict scenarios with reasonable accuracy,
marked by an overall MACE F1 score of 0.408. This achievement suggests that the
combination of naturalistic data collection and human annotation, paired with
automatic deep learning inference, has significant potential to process massive
amounts of data, thus accelerating autonomous driving research. The SceNDD dataset
is available for download at: https://github.com/FujiApp/SceNDD.git. This study

at ICMLA 2021 under the title CoDD. Moreover, our research was presented at

Our research delves into how everyday people, along with occasional users of the Signal messaging app, understand the concept of PINs. We conducted a study consisting of 216 participant interviews to explore this understanding. Our analysis reveals that even occasional users of Signal have some idea of what PINs are, but often struggle to explain their purpose. Interestingly, enthusiastic Signal users tend to have a more accurate understanding of PINs, viewing them as a security measure. In contrast, occasional users are often ambivalent towards PINs, seeing them as an unnecessary aspect of the app. To inform design decisions that effectively cater to a broad range of users, including both enthusiastic and occasional users, our recommendations emphasize the need to enhance app security by making visible and appealing existing security features, while introducing more user-centered methods for managing PINs. Our findings can also serve as a starting point for future research on enhancing security within communication apps. A secondary analysis of user comments from the Signal feedback forum adds depth to our understanding of users' thoughts on PINs. Ultimately, our research aims to provide insights that Signal designers can use to improve user comprehension of PINs and other similar features. This research proposes a new method of calculating the total energy emitted by the sun reaching the earth's surface by using a Gaussian quadrature technique. Estimating the pose of objects in still images is a complex problem that has not been fully resolved. Unlike 3D object reconstruction, our focus is on predicting the orientation of objects in 2D images. While significant advancements have been made, most methods rely on large, class-balanced training datasets. However, images in the wild often contain classes that are under-represented or absent from training datasets, making accurate pose estimation challenging. To address this issue, we introduce a novel technique for zero-shot, class-level pose estimation. Essentially, we propose two novel loss functions: one for pose and another for appearance that do not require pre-trained class-specific templates. Instead, our approach leverages the inherent structural information within the Scene3D++ dataset to train network weights accurately without needing separate data for each class. Our method achieves exceptional results on the YCB video dataset and performs competitively on the T-6D pose estimation dataset. Additionally, we provide further ablation studies to validate our method. Code and pre-trained models can be accessed at the provided link. Although current traffic forecasting models can work well up to a certain point in time, their performance significantly degrades as the forecasting time increases. Typically, traffic conditions repeat at intervals of a few hours or more, and models can utilize patterns from the past to make accurate predictions. A film's marketing effectiveness and unique characteristics are found to be crucial indicators of its box office success,

In the second part of a series of investigations on partially polarized inverse Compton scattering, we explore its potential role in the UV and soft X-ray excess in blazar spectra. This excess in emission is typically observed at shorter wavelengths and higher frequencies in flat spectrum radio quasars, along with other types of quasars and other celestial objects. Low-energy photons from the accretion disk can interact with high-energy magnetic field photons and high-speed electrons in the blazar's jet to produce this excess emission, potentially through the partial polarization of scattering photons. However, since synchrotron radiation is likely to be the dominant emission process in these objects, we expect the magnetic field strength to be quite substantial. Using the MAPPIES program, we developed and ran a Monte Carlo simulation of this scattering process, taking into account the constraints imposed by UV and soft X-ray spectral data. Our simulation, assuming a constant photon field, failed to match the observed spectral shape predicted by this mechanism, primarily due to the limitations of a power law accretion disk blackbody spectrum. A more realistic magnetic field profile might improve the match to observed spectra, likely quantifiable through polarized spectrum analysis. This could provide a significant amount of information about the physical patterns within the blazar's accretion disks. Moreover, varying the magnetic field profile could have a considerable impact on jet spectral shape, balance, and polarization, potentially explaining the observed spectral patterns and polarized light in these objects. This could result in a substantial amount of spectral and polarized flux in the UV and soft X-ray excess in blazar spectra, up to a few GRMSs, an explanation that could be applied to various types of flat spectrum radio quasar spectra. This could be tested through high-resolution X-ray polarimetry and future optical and X-ray spectral and polarimetry investigations. Future high-resolution and high-sensitivity spectroscopic and polarimetric tools are needed to verify these predictions for H- and FSRQ spectra. This potential explanation of the UV and soft X-ray excess in blazar spectra could be significant and should be investigated further. Theory states that no infallible digital identifier for orthogonal pure states can exist if it conforms to two strict conditions: firstly, it must be capable of distinguishing all state configurations, and secondly, it must be compliant with an infinite number of possible state arrangements. However, this theory only holds true for schemes implementing symmetric state encoding methods. This paper presents a digital identifier for symmetric pure states, but with a twist - it can successfully distinguish a finite number of distinct state configurations, even in schemes involving an infinite number of possible state arrangements. Furthermore, this digital identifier can be successfully applied to schemes implementing both symmetric and asymmetric encoding techniques. Finally, this digital identifier can be easily converted into a digital identifier for symmetric pure states, but with a reduced number of distinct state configurations that it can successfully distinguish. Both theoretical analysis and numerical simulations are utilized to verify the performance of the proposed local universal digital identifier. Numerical simulations reveal that it can successfully distinguish up to 8191 distinct state configurations. However, it is worth noting that this number can be increased further. This research underscores that the conclusions drawn from the theoretical analysis of local universal complementary channels are overly restrictive. This is achieved by demonstrating that the locally universal complementary channel defined in this paper can successfully transmit a finite number of distinct signals, even in schemes involving an infinite number of possible state arrangements. This is in direct contradiction to the conventional wisdom that an infallible local universal complementary channel is inherently probabilistic in nature. Furthermore, this achievement is used as the foundation to successfully apply the principle of local reversibility to distinct encoding methods. This is a novel contribution that has not been made before. This research is capable of being extended to the study of local reversibility for distinct encoding techniques involving both real and complex amplitudes. This is a topic that is yet to be explored. Our research examines the direct and indirect consequences of primordial magnetic fields that follow a log-periodic pattern in their variation. This characteristic is seen in how these fields influence the size of cosmic strings and the curvature of space caused by gravitational waves.  To determine the potential for these gravitational waves to be detected, we analyzed their predicted signal in the frequency range of the Pulsar Timing Array. As a result, we found that observations of advanced gravitational wave sources like binary black hole mergers do not provide sufficient insight into the properties of these fields.  Instead, we suggest that gravitational waves from the logarithmic curl of the electromagnetic fields be searched for in data from the Pulsar Timing Array, with forecasts indicating a possible detection potential in the frequency range of $\sim 1-10\times 10^{-9}$ Hz.  A possible side effect of these fields is the induction of an electric field on cosmic strings, which then collapse into black holes, producing gravitational waves with a significant effect on the amplitude of gravitational waves from the Primordial Magnetic Fields.  This effect leads to a relationship between the parameters of these fields and the frequency range of PTAs.  Finally, we found that detecting circular modes separately from the binary signal may be difficult due to their similarity in amplitude and waveform.  On the other hand, the frequency spectrum of the gravitational waves from the Primordial Magnetic Fields is expected to exhibit distinct characteristics such as a clear peak and a 1/f behavior in different frequency ranges.  These predictions suggest that detecting indirect evidence of the primordial magnetic fields may be possible in the near future, long before the detection of the circular modes alone can be confirmed through analysis of the Pulsar Timing Array data.  This finding highlights the potential of the Pulsar Timing Array to serve as a probe of the properties of the cosmological perturbations and the early universe.  This proposal is based on the idea that gravitational waves from the breakdown of symmetries in the early universe can be searched for in the Pulsar Timing Array data.  As a result, a thorough investigation of the Pulsar Timing Array data may yield valuable insights into the characteristics of the primordial magnetic fields and their connection to the early universe.  This discovery may pave the way for a more in-depth search of other breakthroughs in the universe, such as cosmic strings and the force of gravity.  As a consequence, a more detailed search of the Pulsar Timing Array data may yield important insights into the underlying mechanisms of the universe and its composition

Achieving cross-language search between languages that aren't closely related poses significant challenges, and often the state starts with a monolingual query in the less common language. We investigated enhancing cross-language information retrieval tasks by using ensembles of vector-based cross-LC models that incorporate interactive and non-interactive frameworks. By utilizing query and document embeddings from two architectures, we demonstrated the superiority of our proposed method over existing approaches. We assessed our method's performance using a diverse set of languages, including Indo-European, Sino-Tibetan, and Niger-Congo languages, as well as multilingual and monolingual settings, obtaining notable improvements in terms of precision and mean average precision compared to the existing state-of-the-art model, especially for less commonly used languages. We found that the success of our proposed method largely depends on the quality of available monolingual data, and we discussed potential strategies to improve our method for languages with limited resources, including data augmentation and semi-supervised learning techniques. We also addressed various limitations and potential biases of our method, emphasizing the importance of further research to overcome its current restrictions. The proposed method and its associated data and code are publicly available on our GitHub page, along with additional resources. We believe that our study contributes significantly to advancing cross-LC research, particularly for less commonly used languages with limited resources. We further explored the current capabilities and limitations of existing state-of-the-art cross-LC models by conducting in-depth analysis and interpretation of model predictions, and we demonstrated the benefits of our method not only through numerical assessments but also through qualitative analysis and human evaluation. We observed notable improvements in less commonly used languages, and our study sheds light on the importance of interactive frameworks in cross-LC tasks, while also highlighting opportunities for future research to overcome current limitations. Finally, we introduced new methods for automatic evaluation and human annotation, and we hope that our work enables other researchers to build upon our findings. We are committed to releasing our code and data to the public on our GitHub page, and we welcome other researchers to replicate and advance our study. We conducted an initial human evaluation to assess our method's performance and provide insights for future research, and we are prepared to repeat it in the future. The human annotation process is currently available on our GitHub page, and we are happy to share it with other researchers. We also plan to integrate our method with existing search engines and engage in further research, and we are committed to disclosing our results and code to the public. This sequence of events is part of a larger star formation cycle, but the details of the transition from pre-stellar core to protostellar object remain a topic of much debate. Recent studies, however, suggest this transition involves a dynamic process of instability and balanced forces, which can be observed through the analysis of pre-stellar cores in Ophiuchus and Taurus. This research aims to model and interpret the observed properties of these cores by applying principles from hydrostatic stability, taking into consideration the cooling and thermal properties of the cores as well as the role of magnetic fields. A new model of the pre-stellar core collapse has been developed, which reveals that the cores can be unstable and may eventually form a rotating, accreting protostar. This could explain the observed spread in mass of low-mass protostars and may also be relevant to the formation of planets, particularly those in the mass range of super-Earths and terrestrial planets. This research also points to a surprising connection between the study of low-mass star and planet formation, suggesting that the mass of a star or planet could be influenced by the efficiency of the accretion process. During the night of September 18, 2018, the Large Binocular Telescope's on-agument observatory accompanied an observation of the moon's eclipse as it passed through the B, V, R, and I filters. These observations provided a valuable resource to assess the impact of atmospheric conditions on photometric transformations between different wavelengths. By comparing light curves from the eclipse event with theoretical models of the Earth's shadow, researchers were able to determine the ratio of I to V, R to V, and V to B band magnitudes under diverse atmospheric conditions. Additionally, the on-agument observations of this eclipse provided a unique opportunity to analyze temporal variations in the response ratio, which describes the alteration in a system response over a specified period. In this study, the on-agument observations of the eclipse serve as a foundation to develop a method for detecting atmospheric changes in real-time based on a moving average algorithm and a wavelet statistical method. This approach leverages the moving average and wavelet statistical methods to identify and mitigate fluctuations within a 30-minute time frame. Furthermore, the study presents a comparison of atmospheric models developed using the I to V, R to V, and V to B band magnitude ratios. Ultimately, the study demonstrates the effectiveness of the Large Binocular Telescope's on-agument observations and atmospheric models in accounting for atmospheric variations under diverse conditions. These on-agument observations and atmospheric models have been incorporated into the Quick Atmospheric Variability Filter software, which utilizes the moving average and wavelet statistical methods to mitigate atmospheric fluctuations in real-time. This quick AVO filter is a key component of the Large Binocular Telescope's Extreme Precision Transit Survey initiative. Moreover, the technique has been successfully applied to observations taken by the TRAPPIST-e on 2019 September 27, TRAPPIST-e on 2020 March 5, and the star HAT-P-7 on 2019 September 27. These results were obtained using the TRAPPIST-S, the BISTRO, and the NRES spectrographs, respectively. The TRAPPIST-S and NRES spectrographs are grisms that split the light into its constituent wavelengths, while the BISTRO spectrograph is a polarizer that splits the light into its polarization states. Although the study primarily utilizes broadband filters, the results can be extended to narrow-band filters provided that the wavelength shift between the filters is known in advance. Furthermore, the study reveals that atmospheric corrections are obligatory for accurate photometric transformations between filters characterized by a substantial R to B band response

This generalized logic does not follow standard logical rules when dealing with certain constructs, such as the Stone representation of certain algebras. Additionally, Pontryagin duality does not provide a straightforward equivalence for certain logical concepts between the original and the dual spaces in this context. The paper also makes some observations about using dual spaces as a model for certain computational logics. A novel challenge has arisen with the growth of Federated Learning (FL), a method that gathers participant devices to train a centralized model without revealing confidential information to a third party. Although FL initially aimed to enhance privacy and fairness, the equitable nature of its aggregated gradient-based algorithm remains unexplored until now. This research delves into how FL's aggregated gradients influence the model's accuracy and fairness when trained with diverse data and examines a method to measure individual contributions to the aggregated model. Furthermore, the study investigates the connection between FL's training process and its fair and private outcomes, considering a fairness metric known as Demographic Disparity (DD) and a privacy framework called Differential Privacy (DP). The research reveals that achieving both fairness and privacy is a complex task, requiring a higher DP level resulting in significantly worse model performance, even precluding the use of FL in certain domains where high DD persists, such as in the training data for speech models involving minority population labeling. Potential future directions for FL, based on recent advances in Fair and Private Machine Learning, are discussed. The research method and its associated code have been made available on our GitHub page at https://github.com/lethienhan76/Fl-agr- fairness-and-disp. This research ultimately highlights FL's limitations in real-world domains with high DD measures and demonstrates the need for further research in incorporating fairness and privacy considerations into FL development. Protecting WPT receivers from this interference requires the deployment of intelligent surface units (ISUs) to redirect the interference signal, which however poses an optimization problem for maximizing overall network throughput. In models that suggest dark energy and leptogenesis share the same fundamental properties, the lightest superheavy scalar acts as a common ingredient. By combining insights and results from cosmology and particle physics, the minimum requirements for achieving the right amount of dark energy and leptogenesis within our universe can be pinpointed. Our study focuses on a particular type of model, the scalar-mediated leptogenesis with a conjugate symmetric potential, to determine the minimum requirements for achieving the observed universe density of dark energy with a cosmological constant, as well as the correct baryon asymmetry through leptogenesis. By thoroughly analyzing the minimum requirements, the possible dark energy density contribution is constrained, resulting in a upper limit of $\Omega_{\phi} \lesssim 0.12$ based on low-energy experimental data. Furthermore, the study highlights how additional mechanisms can be employed to lower the required scalar mass, thereby increasing the upper limit on dark energy density. Possible upper limits of $\Omega_{\phi} \lesssim 0.06$, $0.07$, or $0.08$ are considered in the presence of radiative corrections, memory leakage, and the alignment mechanism, respectively. Finally, the study explores how a future measurement of the neutrino mass by KATRIN could influence the understanding of dark energy within this model. Measuring a neutrino mass of less than 0.8 eV would strengthen the constraint on dark energy density, whereas a measurement of greater than 1 eV would lead to a revised upper limit of $\Omega_{\phi} \lesssim 0.05$. In summary, the study of dark energy properties emerges as a crucial area of research in this model, with a wide range of possible values, from $10^{-2}$ to $10^{-4}$, making it significantly lower than the density of matter but substantially higher than the density of radiation. By characterizing dark energy within this model, the study reveals a fundamental relationship between dark energy and leptogenesis that could significantly advance our understanding of fundamental particle and cosmological processes. While this relationship may not be sufficient on its own, it could serve as a valuable starting point for future research and potential discoveries. Moreover, the study demonstrates that achieving a deeper understanding of dark energy within this model could also lead to significant breakthroughs in particle physics and leptogenesis. Ultimately, the study highlights the importance of a well-informed cosmological research program that could significantly advance our understanding of dark energy and its intricate connections to fundamental particle physics processes. This research introduces OLODB, a novel object detection framework centered around text objects. Unlike standard object detection datasets, OLODB features an unconventional set of bounding-box annotations. Instead, it utilizes lexicon-based image feature extraction, followed by a specially tailored loss function. As a result, OLODB can function without these annotations, relying on pseudo-boxes generated by clustering instead. Our findings show that although individual components of OLODB are previous approaches repurposed, the combination of features resulting from this innovative architecture upgrade marks a substantial improvement over current methods. Notably, OLODB surpasses state-of-the-art word detection models when evaluated on the ICDAR 2013 dataset. Furthermore, with a minor adjustment to the model, OLODB achieves comparable performance on the larger ICDAR 2015 dataset, outshining state-of-the-art word detection models there as well. As a natural extension of OLODB's capabilities, we also demonstrate its ability to accurately identify individual characters within retrieved text segments. Consequently, OLODB represents a significant step toward a complete, character-based visual text recognition system. Predicting insurance policyholders' probability of death over a specified time period is a critical problem that has significant financial implications for insurers. Achieving accurate predictions relies on effectively modeling population mortality rates, which are influenced by various factors. To address this challenge, we propose a novel approach that employs a factor model with time-varying parameter loadings. By allowing the model to adapt to changes in its factor loadings over time, it can better account for the diverse mortality risks among policyholders and capture the varying trends in rates over time. Using data from multiple life insurance policies, we demonstrate the superiority of our proposed approach compared to alternative models with static factor loadings. Furthermore, we evaluate the performance of our model through both theoretical analysis and practical application. The results reveal that a factor model-based method outperforms actuarial methods, such as the average age approach, in providing accurate mortality predictions. Moreover, our model surpasses a recent machine learning method in terms of predictive accuracy. Lastly, our research also explores the ability of our model to forecast mortality rates at different intervals using data from multiple policies. The results highlight the importance of considering non-linear and time-varying factors in predicting mortality rates. Overall, our work contributes to the development of an innovative machine learning-actuarial method for mortality prediction, which has the potential to be applied not only to insurance policies but also to broader demographic analysis. One major hurdle preventing widespread adoption of neural architecture search (NAS) is the high computational cost. In this research, we investigated this cost and identified that NAS models often produce redundant information that contributes to the expense. We specifically analyzed the R2Soft Actor-Critic (R2SAC) model, which has shown efficient search results or reduced computation time. Our analysis uncovered that R2SAC' efficiency mainly stems from avoiding exploring unfavored candidates rather than searching only necessary samples. We then introduced an optimized version of R2SAC, incorporating an attention mechanism to filter data selectively. This modified model significantly lessened its computation cost while maintaining the majority of its original performance. As a result, it can perform multiple (three or four) consecutive training rounds within a typical NAS framework. We evaluated our approach with multiple datasets, including CIFAR10, CIFAR100, and ImageNet, and our findings confirm that it can autonomously discover well-performing architectures comparable to or better than state-of-the-art models, with significant cost reductions of up to 72.44% in training time and 79.16% in validation accuracy assessment. These results suggest that by using an optimized version of R2SAC with additional rounds of training, one can achieve more reliable and efficient results. Time series analysis involves extracting valuable insights from data collected at specific intervals with inherent meaning. When examining time series, it is crucial to acknowledge that measurements may be taken at random points, rather than at predetermined times, which can impact whether initial trends persist in the future. When dealing with uncertain time points, a common solution is to use weighted average for proper data representation. This type of time series, known as a weighted random time series, can be utilized in statistical inferences by generating multiple simulated datasets based on existing data. Although tools for this purpose are limited, we have developed an R package to facilitate generating attribute-based random time series, which allows for the creation of data similar to the real data without any necessary condition. This package provides a range of functions to accurately estimate key time series metrics and create confident intervals/regions. We have demonstrated the package's capabilities through practical examples, which demonstrate how to use the package to both expand existing datasets and compare predicted forecast models. This approach allows for the creation of confident, accurate results in situations where traditional methods break down. Furthermore, our method is versatile in that it can be applied to various types of functions, not just the ones that follow a specific mathematical structure. This presents an innovative, groundbreaking technique to handle data in a novel, effective way. This research presents a trustworthy method for evaluating human translators based on Bayesian principles. Traditionally, assessing human translators relies on metrics like BLEU, which measures the similarity between a machine translator's output and a human translation deemed reference. In contrast, our Bayesian approach views translation quality as a Bayesian belief updating problem, where a translator's input serves as evidence to inform a prior understanding of their proficiency. We demonstrate that the reliable measurement of human translators can be achieved by generating multiple machine translations, using the mean translation as a baseline for comparison with human translations in terms of translation quality. Our measurements are then compared across various contexts, including the use of different machine translation models with distinct capabilities and levels of reliability. We also showcase the practical implications of our trustworthiness method in three applications: adjusting the level of complexity of machine translations, adapting translations to specific domains, and refining translation models. Our findings indicate that our approach successfully determines the reliability of translators. Moreover, our rely-on-bayes method has achieved the state-of-the-art performance in terms of accuracy for most experimental settings, even outperforming the top previous methods in some cases. We have also observed that our method achieves competitive results while only using a minimal number of machine translations, namely two, which is particularly suitable for scenarios involving limited resources. We have thoroughly tested our rely-on-bayes method with a substantial dataset comprising 50K Chinese-to-English sentence pairs and conducted an in-depth analysis of its dynamics. We have validated the generalizability of our approach by translating English content to other languages, specifically Russian and Spanish. Furthermore, our method has been found to be robust against the challenges of noisy data. We have performed an extensive set of comprehensive experiments to confirm that our rely-on-bayes evaluation method is efficient in terms of computational complexity. We have successfully demonstrated the applicability of our evaluation to a diverse range of scenarios, effectively answering a crucial question in the field of machine translation: How reliable is a machine translator? Our study provides actionable insights: which translation approach is more reliable? Which domain requires the most translation expertise? Which translation model is most effective? We have achieved these breakthroughs by pioneering a novel evaluation metric that is trustworthy, efficient, and versatile, effective in most contexts, computationally simple, and applicable across various domains. Through theoretical analysis, our findings indicate that even a random neural network in its raw state has the ability to effectively predict basic data patterns, and upon training, can significantly improve its performance. Consequently, it's found that the performance of our model scales better than that of CNNs, which require adjustments to parameters such as filter size and stride to effectively predict patterns. We investigate the characteristics of the two-dimensional Fermi polaron model, where a single impurity is attracted to a sea of Fermi particles, under conditions where the impurity's effective mass is infinitely strong or weak. To achieve this, a novel Monte Carlo technique is developed by integrating analytical diagrammatic calculations, yielding a comprehensive polaron energy formula incorporating various many-body effects. By extending the standard variational method, our approach, called diagrammatic Monte Carlo, offers a general tool to generate increasingly accurate variational solutions. Through extensive two-dimensional calculations, we uncover new information about polaron properties, including the ground-state energy, relative motion, and critical temperatures of polarons and bipolarons, which have been theoretically and experimentally sought for decades. The findings demonstrate a strong interplay between the impurity's motion and the collective density fluctuations of the Fermi sea. By comparing our results to recent three-dimensional polaron studies, we uncover an intriguing universal correlation emerging between the two-dimensional and three-dimensional polaron models. Furthermore, our technique is shown to be applicable to other attractive Fermi systems, providing a link to ongoing and future experiments on ultracold fermionic atoms and two-dimensional materials, such as hexagonal boron nitride, where the formation of polarons and bipolarons via strong interactions is theoretically predicted. Our work enables the quantitative explanation of key features of polaron physics and sets the stage for investigating more complex interacting systems, including superconductivity and other complex many-body phenomena. The ground-state energies of polaron and bipolaron solutions derived in this work are publicly available and part of established nature-inspired research initiatives that promote collaborative understanding between natural and theoretical phenomena. In mesh networks, mesh routers update firmware periodically to maintain the network's stability.  Unlike traditional update methods, where updates are made across the network immediately after a router's firmware has been updated,  Mesh networks pose a problem.  A partially updated mesh router interferes with its mesh neighbors, causing network instability.  A reliable update approach for mesh networks,  called INET-FU,  enables mesh routers to delay firmware updates until all routers have updated their firmware safely.  INET-FU utilizes a pre-update check to assess potential updates' impact on mesh routers.  A real-world evaluation was conducted on a 379-mesh router network that utilized OpenWRT,  based on a 3-month period of  2497 firmware changes involving 17 distinct models.  A comparison was drawn between INET-FU's performance and a traditional FU approach.  A simulation study demonstrated that if the traditional FU approach was used,  firmware updates could result in a 17% probability of mesh routers falling back to older versions.  A 99.99% level of confidence was established through rigorous testing that INET-FU successfully prevents mesh router rollbacks in both the real-world evaluation and simulation.  A further investigation revealed that a critical factor contributing to mesh router failures after FU is closely linked to CPU usage.  A second firmware optimization technique, called power-cycling,  was then proposed to minimize mesh router failures caused by FU.  A comprehensive evaluation was conducted comparing INET-FU plus power-cycling to INET-FU alone,  showcasing an additional 71% reduction in mesh router failures brought about by INET-FU.  A thorough analysis was then carried out to establish a relationship between the cost of failure and the time it takes for a mesh router to recover.  Open-source code for INET-FU and power-cycling has been created and it is going to be a part of the Model-SIM framework,  found at https://github.com/ericpeng123/model-sim.  The model also includes realistic latency,  models human behavior,  simulates FU at different time intervals,  and it accounts for a large mesh router failure rate equal to 1%.  The simulation code can be found at https://github.com/ericpeng123/fu-sim.  A detailed tutorial on how to utilize the simulation code has been created at https://github.com/ericpeng123/fu-sim/wiki/Tutorial.  A copy of this document has been submitted to Cisco Systems

High voltage direct current lines can be built to connect renewable energy sources to a power grid, but the strategy behind their placement is crucial. The choice of specific locations can greatly affect the benefits they provide, with potential losses being overlooked in current decision-making processes. This could ultimately lead decision-makers to rely on inefficient methods, such as random selection, to determine optimal hookups, rather than strategic placement. A study model, including all major components of system integration, has been developed to test the impact of different development scenarios on the efficacy of power transport links. Various non-optimized methods were also introduced to compare the outcomes, one of which involves extending the existing transport network in a radial pattern from high capacity energy regions. Results show this approach leads to reduced energy transport losses and higher energy sharing capabilities in comparison to a random hookup scenario. However, further optimization is required to reveal the full benefits of these power transport networks. A more precise optimization method, including a comprehensive ranking of power transport losses, is currently under implementation. When this approach is finalized, it will allow for a comprehensive evaluation of power transport networks and their capabilities, providing valuable insights to inform efficient network expansion. This research has significant implications for how power transport networks are managed and will ultimately contribute to a more efficient and effective process for network development. The rules involve either tripling the number and adding one or simply taking one, and the conjecture suggests that no matter what initial value is chosen, the rules will always result in a sequence that ends at zero. Current summary evaluation methods fall short due to several limitations, leading to a failure to fully capture the quality of a summary. This paper introduces SummScore, a comprehensive evaluation metric that effectively captures a summary's nuances. Cross-encoder technology is the foundation of SummScore, allowing the model to compare a summary with the source material to determine similarity. This similarity is then converted into a score by training SummScore on a vast dataset of scored examples. To ensure a diverse range of summary types, SummScore is trained on two distinct datasets. This approach yields a score that effectively captures various aspects of a summary's quality. Experimental results across seven diverse summary datasets indicate that SummScore outperforms existing evaluation methods in most cases, particularly for abstractive and highly abstractive summaries. Furthermore, we observe a significant correlation between SummScore scores and human assessment ratings. This study also highlights the importance of considering a summary's relevance to the source material in full-length summary evaluation. In software engineering, suggestions from tools are often considered inferior and untrusted, a sentiment that is reflected in the frequent removal of such suggestions by developers. To better understand this phenomenon, our system has been designed to track suggestions from developers in design dialogues with an underlying intent. By training on these marked dialogues, our system can then predict a developer's intent in new dialogues, aiming to identify when software developers consider suggestions to be untrusted and discard them. By testing our system's conclusions against both internal and external judgments, our results demonstrate that our method provides valuable insights into the untrusted decisions made by software developers. Unlike previous machine learning approaches that often rely on inaccurate software engineering data, our work focuses on the consistent conclusions drawn by software engineering experts. By training on the underlying intent behind developer actions and predicting conclusions at the sentence or screen level, our system has been able to achieve significantly better results compared to the existing state-of-the-art, demonstrating an impressive 93% overall accuracy. To facilitate further research, all of the data that was collected and trained for this study will be made publicly available. Furthermore, our work has identified two key areas that are set to become prominent in the study of design dialogues: the study of developer intentions and the study of software engineering decision-making processes. By exploring these topics, future research can be guided and new perspectives emerge. As future work, we propose exploring developer intentions in design dialogues beyond just trust and plan to investigate this in our next steps. Moreover, our system can be adapted to various other areas of software engineering that are also based on design dialogues, providing valuable insights and helping in the understanding of decision-making processes. To illustrate this, we have tested our system on a dataset from minesweepers, and the results show that our system is effective in predicting the intent behind design dialogues. Ultimately, by following the trailblazing path set by past research on mining design dialogues, our work aims to bring software engineering into the realm of NLP. To begin with, our system has effectively applied natural language models to conclude the intent behind design dialogues. To facilitate further research, we will be releasing all of the data that was collected and trained for this study, and new research can benefit from this in the future. In recent years, SPARQL machine translation has received growing attention as a method to translate queries between languages utilizing graph data structures. SPARQL machines, built on top of graph neural networks, have been used to develop various models for this purpose. A key requirement for SPARQL machines is the ability to process diverse and complex knowledge base data. However, current SPARQL machine models typically train and utilize separate components for the query and knowledge base adaptors, and the resource-constrained training of these components often leads to inefficiencies. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel training technique called duplicate mechanism to enhance the performance of SPARQL machine components within a graph neural network framework. This mechanism allows for the improvement of query component accuracy by promoting uniqueness in query results and minimizing redundant information. We validate the effectiveness of our proposed method through both theoretical analysis and experimental testing on multiple datasets. To the best of our knowledge, this research represents the initial exploration of duplicate mechanisms for SPARQL machines. Our study demonstrates the potential of duplicate mechanisms to elevate the overall effectiveness of SPARQL machines. The method and data can be accessed at: https://github.com/baizhangxi/SPARQL-NMT_duicide. Additionally, the research has been published in: Z. Xi, Y. Li, and M. Zhou, SPARQL-NMT Duicide: Enhancing SPARQL Machine Translation with Duplicate Mechanism, In Proceedings of the 2022 International Conference on Data and Knowledge Engineering (ICKEE 2022), June 2022.

For researchers making publishing decisions, the quality of a venue is a crucial factor, impacting not only the impact of a paper but also the impact of the venue itself.  While the impact factors are susceptible to variation, a paper's citation count is only indirectly indicative of a venue's quality.  A more accurate measurement of a venue's quality can inform researchers and influence impact factors, thereby modulating the impact landscape.  Existing methods for assessing venue quality focus on analysis either retrospective or predictive.  To develop a more accurate model, we suggest examining key characteristics of a venue, including its size, defined by the number of publications, and the concentration, characterized by the entropy of their distribution across different fields and journals.  We discovered significant differences in the size and concentration of venues recognized for their prestige.  To evaluate our proposal, we applied our method to a large dataset consisting of 1.9 million papers published between 1950 and 2017 from the Web of Science, and we found that the combination of size and concentration can effectively distinguish between top and low-quality venues up to 85% and 80% of the time respectively.  Our technique is then used to investigate how the quality of a venue affects a paper's outcome and examines the relationship between a paper's impact and the concentration of a venue.  Our analysis reveals that a more concentrated venue is associated with stronger interdisciplinary connections and higher citations.  Based on these observations, we examine the temporal evolution of the quality of a venue by tracking the variation in its size and concentration over time.  Next, we compare the growth patterns of the quality of a venue with its growth in citations and other key characteristics like the number of papers and the number of authors.  Our analysis reveals that a paper's venue's growth is distinct from a paper's growth and also from the growth of a paper's citations.  To test the real-world applicability of our method, we applied it to select Digital Libraries and discovered that a systematic evaluation of a paper's venue based on its size and concentration can be very beneficial in making publishing decisions. We further explore autonomous sets and develop a faster algorithm to find the maximum-weight autonomous set in a given graph. Our analysis also addresses the existence and efficacy of efficient graph standardization methods for graphs characterized by high degree variability. Specifically, our results show that in graphs exhibiting significant degree disparities, instances of smaller size may not benefit from graph standardization, whereas those of larger size may see improved results. We utilize edge list representation for our analysis and implementations. Our findings are accompanied by experimental validations on real-world social network datasets. In particular, our research shows that in graphs characterized by high degree variability, over-standardization can actually harm performance. Additionally, through experimental analysis, we establish that degree variability is a critical factor determining the suitability of graph standardization, and that the method's effect can depend on the specific algorithmic task at hand. Finally, our results illustrate that the performance of the maximum autonomous set and maximum clique algorithms is influenced by graph standardization, and that in certain cases, over-standardization can lead to reduced performance. We conclude that the benefits of graph standardization are not always universal and dependent on specific criteria such as input representation, task at hand, etc. Moreover, our research showcases the computational efficiency of edge list representation in comparison to adjacency matrix for certain tasks. The discovery of periodic X-ray flares from the close binary system CR Draconis has prompted research on its low-frequency radio emission. Between 2019 and 2021, observations of CR Draconis revealed persistent and low-intensity, millimeter-wave radiation. Owing to its low brightness, this radio emission could be characterized as an extreme source of electron-cyclotron maser (ECM) radiation. It was determined that the radio emission from CR Draconis originates from plasma with electron temperatures ranging from 10,000 to 30,000 K. Interestingly, this low-frequency radiation exhibits a nearly periodic pattern that aligns with the 1.284-day flare activity, but also shows some instances of radio emission occurring out of phase with X-ray flares, sometimes lasting for hours or days. Our findings suggest that the radio emission detected at low frequencies is most likely associated with the bright X-ray flare that takes place on the magnetic field loop structure of the plasma. Additionally, we have identified features such as narrow radio bands, radio comets, and broad bands, all of which can be linked to quasi-steady ECM radiation originating from the plasma. Two types of motion were observed in the radio emission: translation involving rapid movements of radio bands and dot-like structures, as well as supersonic-like drift of radio bands, characterized by speeds that exceeded standard drift speeds by an order of magnitude. Our analysis of CR Draconis supports the notion that magnetic tension leads to the compression of the current layer at the X-point, resulting in the presence of two reconnection regions that give rise to the observed radio emission. Moreover, this compression causes a significant increase in the magnetic field component perpendicular to the current sheet, resulting in the observed narrow radio bands. In certain instances, we have also identified the emergence of radio emission associated with the quasi-equilibrium state of plasma, characterized by electron temperatures ranging from 10,000 to 30,000 K, and a magnetic field component parallel to the current layer that can be sufficient for supporting stationary plasma configurations. Our research supports the notion that the radio emission from CR Draconis originates from plasma with the aforementioned stationary properties. Finally, our analysis suggests that the mechanism driving low-frequency radio emission in CR Draconis involves quasi-steady ECM radiation, resulting from the compression of the current layer at X-points of flaring magnetic field configurations. There's a significant distinction between the ways humans and machines interpret visual alterations, especially in extreme cases. This disparity becomes apparent when exploring intense image transformations, which people can easily perform on images without the assistance of computers. These transformations, which include rotations beyond 360 degrees, essentially render the objects within the scene indistinguishable from one another. Surprisingly, machines struggle to recognize objects undergoing intense transformations, just like humans but computers use a different approach, relying on object parts rather than evaluating context like people do. This research's goal is to investigate how intense visual transformations affect both humans and machines, with a particular focus on the different ways they respond to these changes. By doing this, we're exploring a new class of intense image distortions, which retain its meaning even after intense local transformations, thus allowing us to compare machine and human perception in a more natural setting. Ultimately, this work highlights the value of exploring intense visual transformations that are both meaningful to humans and manageable for machines, which in turn enables us to develop more effective models that capture the complexity of human vision. The research shows that machines can learn to classify objects undergoing intense transformations but only when the objects in question have been extensively annotated by humans. This annotation facilitates pattern extraction that mirrors human vision more closely. Additionally, we found that machines perform better when focusing on a narrower range of intense transformations, which helps reduce spatial distortions. Interestingly, this research sheds light on the different ways humans and machines represent objects, with machines more prone to identifying objects based on their visual attributes rather than context. This research was tested using various image classification tasks and machines, with notable results including an impressive 4% improvement in object recognition on a specific computer vision challenge when using our proposed methods.
