The pursuit of ultrafast lasers capable of producing high-energy pulses through Kerr-lens mode-locking faces significant challenges in high-power systems. Fundamental limitations arise from the nonlinearity of this technique and the inherent trade-offs it imposes. A combination of linear losses and higher linear gain leads to lower threshold currents and higher pulse energies, but this relationship is complicated by pulse breakup and loss of energy in the laser cavity. To better understand Kerr-lens mode-locking, we investigate its underlying physics and explore ways to optimize Kerr-lens lasers. Our analysis begins by examining the critical beam radius in a homogeneous gain medium and comparing it to that achieved with a beam that has already been focused, revealing the optimal conditions for maximum gain. We also discuss the strategy of incorporating an x-ray preamplifier to overcome the limitation of low energy output and subsequent high-loss recovery methods to enable high-energy pulse generation. Our study also examines the role of Kerr-lens mode-locking in soliton generation and transits through a resonator, highlighting the complex phenomena of soliton breakup and regeneration, and the unique time and frequency properties of the solitons. Finally, we have identified the conditions required for achieving soliton compression and have outlined a comprehensive approach for building high-energy pulse sources. The analysis is reinforced by detailed numerical simulations of real-world soliton compressors. By offering a valuable historical perspective and comparative analysis of Kerr-lens mode-locking and other nonlinear laser techniques, our study provides a deeper understanding of the principles and challenges involved in high-energy ultrafast laser systems. It lays a solid foundation for future research and development of high-energy pulse sources with vast potential applications. The analysis is further complemented by a detailed review of high-energy pulse lasers and x-ray sources, which are essential for cutting-edge scientific research. The corresponding numerical models, code and data are available for the reader to replicate and extend our research. The geometric approach to understanding Kerr-lens mode-locking provides a durable and timeless foundation that can be adapted and applied to a broader range of nonlinear laser techniques and future high-energy pulse laser and x-ray source developments. In vast networks with numerous interactions, our task is to predict new connections based on community structure and long-term relationship patterns, while also optimizing resource usage by developing efficient algorithms.  We address this by employing a Scalable Super Node Transformer (SSNT), which effectively captures global network characteristics in sparse networks, and contributes to two areas. Second, it expands the application of super node transformer to sparse networks, making it suitable for a broader range of real-world data.  We validate our approach through multiple experiments and comparisons using various networks with different characteristics, and the implementation is available for public use.  Notably, our research reveals that certain existing algorithms, designed for sparse networks, can actually degrade performance on more sparse data, while also consuming excessive time with no noticeable improvement.  This highlights a fundamental issue where current methods are not optimized for sparse networks, and our work addresses this by developing new and efficient algorithms that minimize time and space complexity while producing accurate results.  Conversely, our results show that methods optimized for sparse networks can fall short on more dense data, and this, in turn, inspires future work to adapt current techniques to better fit various network types.  Ultimately, our approach opens up new possibilities for applying super node transformers to sparse data in a more efficient manner.

Although social media use is widespread, detailed analysis of online activity remains limited due to the need for large, well-defined datasets to support such research.  Despite significant efforts worldwide to gather mental health data, valuable research resources remain underdeveloped in this field.  A major social media network's depression-related posting dataset, comprising nearly 4000 social media posts from around 230 users, was collected through a crawler tool.  A small, diverse group of participants provided linguistic ratings of depression severity for each post, and relatedness scores were assigned to define meaningful content for every user.  A user-centric approach was taken to gather context and emotions expressed in online content.  Moreover, user-defined sessions provided temporal context, and experimentally-derived lists of depression-related keywords enabled performance comparison between rule-based and neural network classifiers.  From baseline performance, our depression detection model achieved improvements of up to 14% through trained systems. A straightforward compartmental model is constructed to study the spread of COVID-19, where individuals are divided into four groups: V (vulnerable), S (susceptible), I (infected), and R (recovered). The model assumes that vulnerable individuals become infected at a constant rate, susceptible individuals transform into vulnerable at a steady rate, and infected individuals recover at a constant rate. Furthermore, following recovery, individuals receive immunity that lasts forever. The model takes into consideration the natural deterioration of susceptible and recovered individuals, where the rates of decline are influenced by COVID-19 and aging, respectively. The stochastic version of this model is analyzed using techniques from renewal theory to compute the time until extinction of the vulnerable and infected populations. The time to infection and death is found to be approximately exponential in the early stage. The model is applied to data for Italy, Spain, and the US, providing an empirical validation of the model's predictions and comparing life expectancy with and without COVID-19. The findings indicate that early interventions reduced life expectancy by 10-20 years. The model also enables comparison of death rates, which are found to be significantly higher in the US than in Italy and Spain. Lastly, scenarios involving the impact of social distancing, vaccination, and multiple infections on life expectancy are explored. Findings indicate that social distancing and limited vaccination can prolong life expectancy by several years, while multiple infections tend to decrease the overall life expectancy. The models proposed provide valuable insights for policymakers and medical professionals to inform COVID-19 mitigation and post-pandemic recovery strategies. A time-honored method for comparing two states is the Bellman equation, often used in dynamic decision-making tasks. However, this approach can become unreliable in uncertain environments where future outcomes are highly variable. The resulting Bellman operator may not have a well-defined path independence, making it unsuitable for complex scenarios where multiple possible futures need to be accounted for. In such chaotic systems, researchers have developed an alternative framework by incorporating risk-adjusted measures of uncertainty, known as CAPM, COPSS, or $\rho$-measure. Building on this concept, a new hedging framework is established, Profound Bellman Hedging, by combining a dynamic strategy with a tailored performance metric. Within this context, an optimal hedging process is formulated using the Profound Bellman equation, a recursive formula that describes the optimal results of a hedging process. By defining a Profound Bellman operator, a new hedging framework is established that addresses various uncorrelated and correlated hedging tasks. Achieving reliable, large-scale quantum computing necessitates a cryogenic system capable of providing low temperatures, combining government-grade security with user-friendly flexibility.  Traditional laboratory cold plates are typically designed to accommodate either security or flexibility.  We've developed an innovative cryogenic system, weighing around 300 kilograms, based on a commercially available 400-liter cryogenic vessel and supported by a custom-designed magnetic shielding system.  This system, consisting of a liquid helium and dilution refrigerator setup, provides user-friendly control and is supplemented with superconducting and resistive magnetic fields, along with a range of cryogenic and room temperature electronic interfaces.  We have successfully tested this platform's performance and durability across various large and small scale quantum computers under development at Fermilab, utilizing a variety of superconducting two-dimensional materials for high-performance quantum components.  This platform, dubbed the "quantum pit,' serves as a flexible research and development tool, allowing rapid testing and prototyping of advanced quantum technologies that operate at millikelvin temperatures, backed by comprehensive safety measures and user support.  We discuss the platform's performance in detail, specifically how it maintains a record low 7 millikelvin across its 300 square foot area using a novel extended heat exchanger, and highlight its advanced features, security systems, and operational procedures.  This platform has significantly enhanced the development of quantum computers, allowing a new model based on bosonic qubits to achieve an error rate below one in a thousand.  We believe that open-source collaboration and comprehensive user support are vital for big research projects like this to succeed.  The platform's source code and detailed documentation are publicly available on the Fermilab Quantum Computing GitHub page.  This platform has also received an exceptional level of user feedback, and users are encouraged to share their feedback and join the open-source community to develop the next-generation quantum computers that will lead to breakthroughs in fundamental scientific research and cutting-edge applications.  The platform was initially described in a talk presented at the American Physical Society meeting in March 2022.  We have successfully demonstrated the platform's capabilities and performed large-scale quantum experiments under real conditions, and the platform's current status and future developments are discussed in detail.  The platform's future plans include establishing a user-friendly and flexible test bed for testing a wide array of quantum computing, quantum simulation, and quantum information processing systems, and the platform's capabilities and progress will be shared at conferences, publications, and demonstrations until the final goal is achieved. In seismic imaging, direct hydrocarbon detection is a complex problem. Nonuniform sparse models, such as the sparse self-similar matrix, offer an effective approach for analyzing the structure of seismic data. However, existing learning-based methods for sparse model estimation are limited to special cases or uniform sparse models and are impractical for nonuniform scenarios. We address this limitation by introducing a general learning framework, called NuSPAN, which can accurately estimate the parameters of any sparse model. Our proposed method leverages a Proximal Mean Network, a new artificial neural network, to learn the characteristics of individual columns in the sparse model and colinear ones through self-similarity. The learnable parts can be utilized in various sparse models to handle different nonuniform scenarios. We apply NuSPAN to the sparse self-similar model in the context of seismic reflectivity inversion and validate its effectiveness with numerical examples. Our study shows that NuSPAN outperforms existing methods in terms of sparsity, interpretability, and reconstruction accuracy. Additionally, we demonstrate its ability to handle colinear hidden patterns through visual inspections of the sparse self-similar model. With its high performance and versatility, NuSPAN has the potential to be applied to other nonuniform sparse models and various signal processing tasks. In contrast, historical languages present additional challenges stemming from archaic vocabulary, obsolete grammar, and text scarcity, making it increasingly hard to obtain reliable POS labels. This situation is further complicated by the inherent errors inherent to historical text transcription, which poses an especially significant obstacle for pre-19th century languages. This paper explores the viability of set-valued output for POS labeling in historical language contexts. This proposed approach may serve as a reliable fallback for both contemporary and historical language conservation efforts, particularly in situations where the quality of predicted results is directly impacted by the cost of human supervision. This dissertation seeks to establish a major integrability theorem, known as the Non-Uniform Integrability Theory.  The proposed work builds upon the existing research of by P. J. Fitzpatrick and J. J. Peck, and J. Korte.  The new theory is divided into three significant findings.  

The first result provides an analysis of the non-uniform integrability of sequences of real-valued functions through approximations and representations.  It can be viewed as an extension of the non-uniform integrability of sequences of real numbers, similar to the classical result attributed to P. J. Fitzpatrick and J. J. Peck, applied in a more general context.

The second result offers a non-uniform integrability theorem for functions with varying parameters, based on sequences of real-valued functions.  It serves as an extension to the non-uniform integrability of sequences of real numbers, as explored by P. J. Fitzpatrick and J. J. Peck.

The third result presents an application of non-uniform integrability to the context of real-valued functions, drawing parallels with a conclusion by J. Korte.  Specifically, it demonstrates non-uniform integrability's potential to simplify the calculation of the average value of a function across multiple functions and various measures. 

An essential component of this dissertation is Chapter 2, where it provides an in-depth review of the underlying research necessary to understand the Non-Uniform Integrability Theory.  As an added benefit, this chapter also covers the theory of real-valued functions and provides an extended review of the existing literature.

In Chapter 3, the primary goal is to analyze the non-uniform integrability of sequences of real-valued functions through approximations and representations, expanding on the research of Peck and Korte.  Additionally, this chapter seeks to apply the principles of non-uniform integrability to a new perspective, functions with varying parameters, through the research of Fitzpatrick and Peck.  Finally, this chapter aims to apply the non-uniform integrability theory to a real-valued function context, as explored by J. Korte.

Consequently, this chapter serves as a comprehensive conclusion, summarizing the Non-Uniform Integrability Theory and its key contributions.  An added benefit of this chapter is the exploration of future research opportunities inspired by the underlying theories and applications of non-uniform integrability.  Specifically, this chapter paves the way for future studies on non-uniform moment estimates and Stieltjes integrability.

In the fields of pathology and radiology, image analysis is a core component, 
and reliable communication involving these images and their interpretations is 
crucial. While data exchange standards like high-dicom have been created to 
facilitate this process, issues still arise due to the varied use of DICOM 
axiliar features. To address this, a new path towards creating uniform 
regenerative pathways is being introduced, centered on the DICOM information 
type, 'MR fluorospot', which offers 1000 meaningful attributes for model output 
encoding. As proof of concept, a decision tree has been trained to classify 
emphysema levels in chest X-rays and has undergone clinical validation in a 
real-world setting. 

The proposed method involves a comprehensive evaluation, comparing the 
high-dicom technique to other image annotation methods. The study highlights the 
essential characteristics of model outputs that should be recorded, and how 
such data can serve as a template for discussions around the incorporation of 
new features. Finally, the technical implementation and functionality of 
high-dicom are discussed, with suggestions for future improvements provided.

Recently, P. I. Odzieniec proposed a method of restricting symplectic forms on coadjoint orbits to non-degenerate forms on subsets of tangent spaces. This method involves a specific type of differential form derived from the second adjoint action of a Lie group on its own Lie algebra. In this article, we provide a more direct approach to a specific scenario where a certain differential form, originally found on coadjoint orbits, is transformed into a Clebsch manifold structure. Additionally, we outline the underlying geometric principles that govern Odzieniec's and Celoria's observation, and extend the application to Lie-Poisson structures through the Torquato-Cohen model. Moreover, we demonstrate that systems such as the NLS, QG, and E.1D BO are Clebsch integrable. Lastly, we present a new example of a 2D BO equation that originates from the 2D Toda system. This example is Clebsch integrable and possesses a complete set of integrals. Interestingly, the corresponding Clebsch form results in the appearance of vortex solitons. The related 2D Toda equation bears a significant connection to the 2D chiral Gross-Pitovsky equation. A complete set of integrals for GP equations remains unresolved to this day. This example aims to bridge a crucial gap towards finding a comprehensive solution to the problem. To achieve this goal, we employed a clever manipulation of variables and discovered a previously unknown Poisson structure associated with GP equations, which can be represented as a skew-symmetrizer of a specific matrix. This breakthrough opens doors for the vast applications of techniques like the Nijenhuis operator and multilinear algebras in the field of Clebsch integration. Such techniques initially gained prominence in the works of V. V. Sorin and A. M. Vinogradov. It is worth noting that the Skew-symmetrizer has a more widespread significance extending far beyond Clebsch integration, as it is linked to the geometric principles behind Odzieniec's observation, which were discussed earlier. A decision has been made to maintain the original order of references and include only the works published prior to 2021. A detailed analysis of this example is accompanied by various additional examples of Clebsch integrable systems, which are presented in the preprint 'Clebsch integration of the Zakharov-Sternberg system'. This paper delves into the standard conditions that give rise to entropic discontinuities in systems of conservation laws and explores their contraction in various frameworks, including scalar conservation laws, scalar conservation law systems, and vector conservation laws.  We examine three entropic contraction standards: (1) the scalar conservation law framework, (2) the scalar conservation law system framework, and (3) the vector conservation law framework.  For scalar conservation laws, the standard conditions involve the celebrated Kruzkov entropy, while for scalar conservation law systems, we consider entropies from Kruzkov and the relative entropy between probability measures.  These entropies serve as a basis for defining the entropic contraction condition, which must satisfy certain requirements.  We establish the standard conditions for entropic discontinuities in systems of conservation laws in a comprehensive and interconnected manner, with the scalar conservation law standards being a subset of the scalar conservation law system standards, which in turn are a subset of the vector conservation law standards.  Ultimately, this work's findings on entropic contraction standards in different frameworks provide valuable insights into the development of numerical methods for partial differential equations, especially those relying on probabilistic techniques.  In fact, this work's numerical implications are particularly significant for numerical methods targeting the shallow water and Boltzmann equations.  Furthermore, such results may also facilitate numerical investigations of other equations, such as the FRLEs and the incompressible Euler equations, as well as the creation of novel numerical methods for the fractional shallow water equations.  We plan to explore these applications and advancements in future research.  To maintain clarity and efficiency, some of the numerical implications will be discussed in a follow-up follow-up work. This new scheme is expected to offer superior accuracy and robustness, with the potential to be versatile and adaptable for a wide range of equations, including the mentioned fractional shallow water equations.  We look forward to exploring these opportunities in our future work. To achieve seamless integration with Model Predictive Control (MPC) software, we develop innovative strategies for smoothing out joint position references generated by the MPC algorithm. This is done by using raw data from encoders that capture the actual joint movements but lack sufficient detail due to the inherent limitations of encoder technology. As a result, the MPC algorithm produces position profiles with abrupt changes that may cause damage to robot joints. To prevent this, we introduce two advanced smoothing techniques: (i) an interpolation approach that interpolates between nominal positions obtained from selected key points and actual raw positions, and (ii) a correction method that rectifies robot joint angles by adjusting auxiliary encoder readings during a brief zero-marking operation. Experimental findings for a three-layer industrial robot that incorporates quaternions confirm the efficiency and safety of the proposed methods. Moreover, analytical modeling of the smoothing techniques is carried out and theoretically validated in terms of their influences on the joint motion trajectory. This analysis is facilitated by the application of the Generalized Lissajous Curve model. By providing analytical validation, we address a critical aspect of the algorithm's correctness, paving the way for the development of more complex optimization strategies that go beyond just smoothing the signals. Ultimately, we demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed methods on an NACHI SLUSL 3FA robotic arm by successfully obtaining optimized joint positions that meet the MPC algorithm's smoothness criteria. We introduce a novel approach to address the challenge of modeling molecular dynamics on large time scales, specifically focusing on simulations of O(N) interactions in three-dimensional systems with detailed electrostatics. Our method builds upon Lincoln's multi-site scheme, incorporating a comprehensive quadrature strategy that effectively tackles the complexities of partial charging and non-standard interaction patterns between nearby sites. Our theoretical analysis confirms that the proposed quadrature satisfies key consistency and canonical requirements, thereby facilitating accurate and efficient numerical simulations of linear and nonlinear response dynamics in molecules. Furthermore, our practical evaluation illustrates the advantages of incorporating quadrature-based methods for scaling up multi-site simulations on high-performance computing platforms. Our experimental benchmarks compare the performance of quadrature-based simulations against those using a standard approach on the linear response of a polyene model, demonstrating canonical dynamics on multiple CPU and GPU architectures. Our observed results indicate that the proposed quadrature approach enables accurate and efficient simulations up to significantly higher system sizes than traditional methods. Specifically, we found that quadrature-based simulations can be carried out for much larger molecule lengths relative to the grid size before hitting the canonical limit, resulting in substantial time savings of up to two orders of magnitude. Our study also shows that linear response simulations using quadrature-based methods for a benchmark involving 80 atoms and 160 time steps can be successfully executed on GPU architectures more than two years after the initial publication of the Lincoln model. Our work significantly extends the feasibility of quadrature-based simulations in both theoretical and practical contexts, effectively merging two promising approaches into a single canonical simulation strategy. Our provided source code supports execution on both CPU and GPU architectures, according to the policy of open-source development. The method described in this report has been used in a related publication titled "Electronic coherence is sufficient for generating the nonequilibrium Anderson localization correction in driven systems", available at arXiv:2202.00911. This research examines regional and demographic responses to the pandemic in the United States. A content analysis of nearly 200 online news sources revealed that news sources covering COVID-19 at different rates are also associated with distinct case and death rates in their respective areas. Moreover, the audience reach of news sources is positively correlated with the coverage of COVID-19. By employing a multivariate Bayesian model, our study reveals the interconnections among COVID-19 coverage, case and death rates, and audience size. Interestingly, our results show that a 10% increase in a news source's COVID-19 coverage is linked to a 1% decrease in case and death rates. We also discovered that a 10% larger audience is associated with an approximately 0.15% increase in COVID-19 coverage. The relationships among these variables vary depending on the audience's age and demographic composition. For example, news sources covering a large percentage of children report lower case rates. Similarly, states with older populations have faster declining case rates, and higher income states exhibit lower case and death rates, which in turn are associated with greater COVID-19 coverage. Finally, our study highlights the complex interdependence of media coverage, disease spread, and human behavior, especially in a context where people's pandemic responses are significantly influenced by their trust in information sources. It is crucial for public health officials to recognize and address the substantial impact of information dissemination on public behavior in fighting the pandemic. Ultimately, our study provides valuable insights to news sources and public health officials on how to effectively communicate pandemic-related information to diverse demographic groups. Moreover, our work sets the groundwork for exploring the intricate relationships between information flow and disease spread in real-time, particularly as new waves of the pandemic emerge and vaccine policies unfold. As the pandemic slowly recedes, our study offers a foundation for exploring the connections between news sources, human behavior, and societal well-being in addressing other societal challenges. In the $\vec {p} \to \vec {p}$ elastic scattering process, the level of polarization achieved by the initial polarized proton varies based on the momentum transfer and reaches a maximum at $\tau \approx 0.35$. The final proton also becomes polarized, with its polarization depending on $\tau$ and the mass ratio of $m_n/m_p$. Calculations show that the proton polarization in this process reaches its maximum at a $\tau$ value of around 0.75, with this maximum depending heavily on the neutron to proton mass ratio. A range is estimated for this ratio between 0.999 and 1.003, and corresponding to these values, the final proton polarization achieves its maximum at around $\tau \approx 0.83$ or $0.65$ respectively. A second maximum in polarization occurs for both the initial and final protons at around $\tau \approx 0.9$. The polarizations of the initial and final protons differ the most when $\tau \approx 0.6$ and reach their smallest difference at $\tau \approx 0.9$. The ratio of the width of the polarization maximum to its peak value is similar for both the initial and final protons, with this ratio depending heavily on $\tau$. Calculations of this ratio are found to be consistently around 0.8 * 10$^{-2}$ across different $\tau$ values except for $\tau \approx 0.6$ when it's significantly lower. Further analysis reveals that at $\tau \approx 0.6$, the initial proton achieves its maximum possible squared $Q$-value, while the final proton's energy is lower than its initial state. As a result, its polarization behavior mirrors that of a square root function over this specific $\tau$ value. The minimum possible squared $Q$-value occurs at $\tau \approx 0.9$. The calculated and measured ratios of the Golak factor are used to assess whether an experimentally measured square $Q$-value can be accurately based on a calculation using a Golak factor or whether it needs adjustment to match a square root function over this specific $\tau$ value. An experiment with higher $\tau$ values up to 0.9 is needed to test at Q-values, measured in millibarns, 1 mb, 0.8 mb, 0.6 mb and 0.4 mb respectively, to see if results match the calculation better with or without the Golak factor

A fundamental theory based on a decomposing neutralino as a primary constituent of dark matter is proposed. 
In this framework, a supersymmetric model with $R_{P}$-symmetry is utilized, which naturally prevents mixing between gauginos and fermions due to $R_{P}$ invariance, resulting in zero mixing. 
As a result, the mass matrices of chiral superfields are diagonalized by $R_{P}$-preserving Yukawa matrices, leading to the decomposition of neutralinos, which then lose their supersymmetric counterparts to become a pool of ordinary matter.
The calculated mass spectra of neutralinos indicate that their masses range from a few GeV to several TeV. 
Furthermore, we introduce a model in which the neutrinoless double beta decay amplitude is shown to be proportional to $m_e\lambda^2$, where $m_e$ is the electron mass and $\lambda$ is the strength of baryon number violation. 
This model also predicts that neutralinos at a few GeV within the $R_{P}$-preserving MSSM could potentially account for the invariant amplitudes mediating neutrinoless double beta decay and dark matter, thus providing a consistent explanation. 
Lastly, we discuss the possibility that the superheavy neutralinos at the TeV scale contribute significantly to the photoelectric effect observed from the sun, which could potentially be detected in experiments such as sun-based interferometry and X-ray observatories, allowing for the verification of the proposed dark matter model through astrophysical probes. 
The model also makes another prediction that can be tested: even neutralinos at the TeV scale, which are beyond current experimental reach, could potentially be detected by analyzing the diffuse gamma-ray background at geocentric angles. 
In particular, a prominent emission feature at 40.6 GeV may emerge if the mass of the neutralino contributing to this feature is found to be a few GeV, which is within the reach of future experiments such as CMB-S4, a cosmological probe that will significantly improve the understanding of the cosmic microwave background. 
However, if the mass of the neutralino lies at the TeV scale, which is beyond current experimental reach, a future space-based experiment such as the PRISM project could confirm the proposed model by analyzing the smooth emission background as a function of energy and angle.

Moreover, we investigate the approximation properties of nonlinear combinations of classical NDD operators on the simplest family of multivariate convex sets, and we derive a formula for the asymptotic behavior of nonlinear operator combinations. Finally, this research is extended to approximate general multivariate functions, and we develop a nonadaptive approximation scheme using nonlinear methods. We illustrate the potential applications of these techniques in image processing, and we demonstrate their effectiveness in preserving color details and reducing noise in 24-bit images of the "baboon" and "lena" varieties. This hybrid approach, dubbed ASKOG, leverages the elegance of spectral Koopman methods for nonlinear system analysis while employing sparse grid methods to minimize the computational expense associated with high dimensionality. We derive an error estimation formula and establish convergence rates for ASKOG in the dependence on truncation parameters in various settings. The method's effectiveness is illustrated by its accurate adaptation to the true dynamics in parameter-space geometry. The proposed ASKOG method is expected to serve as a valuable tool for investigating complex parameter-dependent systems. A mathematical approach, the Outward Complex Scaling Method, is described in detail. This method employs a numerical solution to an enlarged set of nonlinear differential equations to calculate the wavefunctions of atoms and molecules in strong direct electric fields. We provide a thorough review of the method's mathematical underpinnings and illustrate its application to a one-dimensional model and the hydrogen atom for one- and two-electron systems, including the effects of polarization on the bound state of the electron in the one-electron case. An important aspect of the method is its ability to determine the critical electric field strength at which the wavefunction diverges into the complex energy plane and to obtain well-beamed continuum solutions representing ionization trajectories. Associated software packages that implement this method for one- and two-electron systems are briefly discussed. We also outline a method for calculating non-adiabatic outward wavefunctions of the electron in the two-electron atom. Lastly, some potential extensions of the method are presented. The Outward Complex Scaling Method offers significant advantages in terms of computational efficiency for calculating high-order correlation energies in strong direct electric fields. We provide the underlying mathematical justification for this method. The linear scaling of the OCS method for one-electron systems is demonstrated analytically. Furthermore, the OCS method's ability to produce well-beamed continuum solutions that facilitate the calculation of high-order correlation energies in strong direct electric fields is illustrated through numerical examples for a one-dimensional model and the hydrogen atom. The method has been successfully extended to two-electron systems, yielding a linear scaling of the four-dimensional OCS equations for the electron, and resulting in well-beamed two-dimensional continuum solutions that accurately model ionization trajectories in the presence of an aligned electric field. These two-dimensional solutions have been used to calculate high-order correlation energies for one- and two-electron systems. The method has been validated by demonstrating agreement with existing literature values. TERS is an advanced form of nano-scale Raman spectroscopy that offers superior chemical sensitivity due to its unique properties. Nevertheless, interpreting the results often poses difficulties due to a combination of factors, including the intricate interplay between electromagnetic and chemical interactions, as well as the complexities inherent in sample and tip configurations. These limitations tend to undervalue the significance of chemical influences, which can significantly impact the sample response. Our research proposes a new computational model that accurately models both electromagnetic and chemical interactions in TERS. This approach relies on a quantum mechanical description of the sample and its components, using a complex superposition of electronic states to account for chemical influences. In contrast, the tip's interaction with the sample is modeled through a scattering-type Green's function, incorporating both propagating and evanescent electromagnetic modes in accordance with the thin-dilutor approximation. Additionally, our model enables the simulation of various tip configurations, including the apodization effect resulting from flatter tips. Our results validate the effectiveness of this approach, providing valuable insights into the relationships between sample properties and TERS spectra. Our findings suggest that chemical influences can have a substantial impact on the sample response, often surpassing the effects of electromagnetic resonance. This breakthrough highlights the importance of considering chemical influences in TERS, thereby refining our comprehension of this technique and its implications for analyzing various types of systems. Our model and results will be made publicly available, allowing researchers to gain a more in-depth understanding of the underlying mechanisms governing TERS sample response. Ultimately, this work is expected to significantly enhance electromagnetic and chemical understanding in TERS, thereby opening new avenues for research and analysis utilizing this technique and its variants such as SERS, STM-Raman, and superconducting qubits. The notion of close neighbor techniques for time series has been developed to identify segments within a time series that resemble neighboring segments from other given series. Several algorithms have been proposed to achieve this, primarily under the dynamic programming framework. Given the high computational demands for close neighbor identification, most existing methods aim to balance efficiency and accuracy. Our study focuses on estimated close neighbor searching under the Frechet distance, considering the inherent limitations of approximation. We propose two new bounds for this purpose, demonstrating their strict inequality properties. Furthermore, we introduce an adaptation of the existing Frechet distance algorithm to identify high-quality approximate close neighbors within a specified threshold, along with an analysis of its time and space complexity. Our method is evaluated using synthetic and real-world data, showcasing its effectiveness and efficiency. The results indicate that our technique can identify close neighbors with a higher quality than previous methods, using the Discrete Frechet distance. A significant finding is that utilizing a constant number of sample points yields a 1.2-approximation of the Discrete Frechet distance, outperform existing methods such as OCNT and reducing their point-prunings-based distortion by approximately 85%. In various quantitative protocols such as quantum sensing and cryptography, inaccurately setting parameter values can lead to unintended consequences, like distorted results and potential security breaches. Error margin in these parameters is known as measurement uncertainty, which, if not addressed, can cause catastrophic quantum sensing data inconsistencies. A newly proposed theoretical framework, the unraveling method, suggests an approach to mitigate measurement uncertainty by effectively eliminating it in theoretical scenarios. However, in real-world applications, this method often relies on unreliable assumptions like independent and identically distributed error correlations. A new technique, the iterative Bayesian unraveling (IBU), builds on the unraveling method while accounting for practical errors by reevaluating the likelihood of data without preconditions. It successively reduces error margins by identifying reliable data subsets, which can be challenging to accomplish in practical experiments. Researchers applied IBU to simulated thermal noise scenarios and compared its performance to conventional techniques like the Monte Carlo and the Markov chain Monte Carlo methods. Interestingly, IBU outperformed these conventional methods in low correlation situations, yet its advancements were hindered by its inability to leverage correlations when they existed. A more advanced version of IBU, dubbed $IBU_\gamma$, was then developed to optimize its performance by incorporating correlations, thereby enabling its application to high-correlation scenarios. When applied to simulated scenarios, $IBU_\gamma$ exhibited superior results by minimizing uncertainty while maintaining accuracy. As robots interact with people in various settings, the likelihood increases that humans will encounter multiple robots. For safe coexistence, humans need to understand and adhere to behavioral expectations that are consistent across different robots. We investigated this issue within the context of a conveying task involving a robot carrying a package, and developed two consistent expectations that emerge when humans and robots collaborate together. Through predictive polls and human-robot interaction, we identified specific robotic standards, such as package removal, and communicated them to participants. Notably, without any prior training, humans who interacted with the robot in a learning-based setting effectively conveyed the package to a significant degree, indicating they had internalized these expectations. We observed that humans who learned to convey the package according to our standards demonstrated better understanding of robotic intentions, specifically by avoiding physical obstacles. These findings contribute to the development of high-level expectations for robot-human collaboration and may contribute to the expansion of safe and efficient collaborative workflows. For tasks like delivery or package tracking, determining routes in unfamiliar territories is a challenge, but with the aid of technology, especially GPS and mapping tools, navigating unknown areas becomes more feasible. GPS technology enables location identification and mapping tools provides topological relationship data, but in cases where GPS signal strength is weak or inadequate map data is available, determining the most efficient route is a complex problem. To address this issue, we have developed a novel solution called HiTMap - a mapping technique that merges topological data with geographical information. By utilizing these maps as guides, we can efficiently calculate routes in known areas, but in unknown territories, our algorithm adapts by selecting key topological nodes and geographical data to optimize route prediction. We have tested our algorithm with a simulated real-world scenario and found that it significantly reduces route search times, with search times being 10 to 20 percent of total route length, and successfully demonstrated our method with a self-driving car experiment. The associated video shows that our algorithm effectively navigates the vehicle through unfamiliar areas without prior knowledge of the environment. The simulation results demonstrate that our algorithm outperforms other current methods by finding more accurate and efficient routes in both known and unknown areas. Building upon existing concepts of scalar functions and corresponding array code sets, we explore the possibility of using multivariable functions to design such codes. Our study is divided into two parts. First, considering the properties of multi-variable functions with a given degree related to a parameter 'q', we demonstrate the existence of a class of inter-family complementary code sets of order (q+1)^k and size (q+1)^k * (q^i +... + q + 1)^k. Additionally, we select a suitable degree of 'q' variable functions and establish the existence of a class of 2-D dual supplementary array code sets of order (q+1)^k and size (q+1)^k * (q^i +... + q + 1)^k. Our approach involves first creating a fundamental code set consisting of linearly independent row-vectors, then iteratively applying a transformation function to generate new code sets, finally ensuring the validity of the constructed codes through the determination of a suitable degree of 'q' variable functions that satisfies both the balance and intersection conditions. Our approach involves a sophisticated mathematical model that breaks down down the process of image formation into two primary steps: the reconstruction of a common CT projection data set that is free of sensor noise, and the decomposition of the noise-free CT data into distinct energy spectra. This model consists of two interconnected variational problems represented by regularized, non-convex minimization problems. To solve this complex mathematical model, we use an iterative algorithm that requires solving two interdependent variational problems at each step. Our approach converges to a stable solution, which we demonstrate through numerical experiments with a selection of phantom and real-life CT data sets. Our results indicate that our method successfully reconstructs noise-free CT data with high fidelity and effectively separates data from different energy sources. This research investigates how electron'spill-over' and nonlocal behavior affect light propagation between two metal spheres connected by a narrow gap. Focus is placed on the smallest possible gaps while maintaining metal continuity.  Different theoretical approaches are compared with an eye towards understanding plasmon-based electronics and optics.  By examining the smallest possible gaps, the spherical structure's symmetry can be maintained, allowing for simplified mathematical analysis.  Various scenarios with different metal sphere configurations are examined, considering both small and large metal spheres.  These studies show that electronic'spill-over' and nonlocal behavior significantly affect electron distribution and electromagnetic field properties, stressing the importance of these factors in these systems.  These results may also influence designs for nanoscale optical and electronic devices, leading to new applications based on these principles.  These findings are planned for publication in the journal Physical Review B following revision.

Displaying the evolution of multiple variables over time can be complex, especially when analyzing large datasets with many such sequences. There are limited visualisation tools and interaction mechanisms that allow for efficient examination of longitudinal data, especially when dealing with datasets that continue to grow. Methods for visualising longitudinal data typically include methodological extensions from movement and time series data analysis but often lack interactive elements. This research proposes a range of design concepts and interactive tools to enhance the visualisation and exploration of longitudinal data, including the use of colour codes, image comparisons and multi-variable sequence time series. Key interactive components include dynamic zooming, focusing on variable subsets, image synthesis and data simulation. This study identifies opportunities, constraints and challenges associated with using screens of time series data and provides design recommendations for researchers and scientists to create effective visualisation tools. An example application, based on data from the German Longitudinal NCHS, is also presented to demonstrate improvements in data analysis and discovery. Analysis results show significant performance gains when using the proposed interactive tools. The research concludes with potential future research directions that combine data analysis and interaction. The paper includes a supplementary online video. The implementation of Graph Neural Networks (GNN) has transformed the healthcare sector by enabling data mixing and learning from complex unstructured data. Nonetheless, existing GNN models are hindered by their inability to generalize medical knowledge acquired from one hospital to another. To address this limitation, researchers have proposed diversifying knowledge representation through GNN. However, few studies have explored enhancing GNN using various types of unstructured data. To rectify this, a new method called Diverse Similarity Graph Neural Network (DSGNN) is being presented, which leverages multiple diverse sources to broaden the knowledge representation of clinical notes. By integrating a diverse-encoder to map multiple diverse sources onto a unified space, DSGNN can synthesize clinical notes from a variety of records. Experimental results demonstrate that DSGNN surpasses state-of-the-art models in text and graph EM detection at MIMIC-III and eICU datasets. DSGNN also yields comparable performance to state-of-the-art models in EM detection using a single hospital record, while outperforming previous research in few-shot learning settings. Furthermore, Ablation Studies prove that the diverse-encoder plays a vital role in DSGNN. As a result, DSGNN can effectively learn and generalize from hospital-specific knowledge while being adaptable to working with clinical notes from a different hospital. Moreover, DSGNN is also capable of working effectively in environments where there is a scarcity of data available for training. The behavior of an electric double layer at the boundary of a charged soft interface is investigated using a pseudo-capacitance model. The effect of a non-uniform solvent polarization on its double electrochemical layer is taken into account. The surface charge density of the interface is influenced by a parameter that represents the extent of solvent polarization. The conductivity of the interstitial medium and the presence of a counter-ion that diffuses in the interstitial region are also considered. A theory has been formulated to describe the soft interface electric double layer, which is verified through the simulation of electrochemical responses such as capacitance, resistance, and faradaic current. The outcome shows that solvent polarization has a significant impact on the electric double layer structure and electrochemical responses, resulting in a decrease in charge transfer resistance and reversible energy storage capacity in comparison to a system without solvent polarization effects. The effect of solvent polarization on soft interfaces is comparable to that of gravitational effects on hard particles, such as nanoparticles and proteins. The research presents an alternative perspective on soft-gravity models, emphasizing the significance of solvent polarization in the electric double layer of soft interfaces. The findings may inspire future experiments on soft interfaces that store energy, leading to novel applications in energy storage. The associated mathematical equations have been made available as supplementary material to facilitate further research in this area. The knowledge and insights presented in this thesis could potentially expand our understanding of electrochemical interfaces and their applications in energy storage and conversion. To overcome this complexity, we propose two efficient, near-optimal algorithms that can be run in either a centralized or distributed network setup. To evaluate these algorithms, we compared their performance with an existing approach as well as a baseline that models no encoding in the network. Extracting information from satellite images has become crucial due to the rapid increase in available data. High-resolution images used in this process contain multiple edge types, including fine details and larger features. A widely employed approach involves employing deep network filters to differentiate between edges. However, these networks often require substantial computation, significant memory, and lengthy training times, limiting their deployment. A more efficient solution involves using only the innermost layer of a pre-trained network, reducing memory usage and edge discrimination costs. Another innovative method utilizes a simplified network built on a residual block, minimizing computational and memory demands while sharing parameters to boost training efficiency. All the proposed network-based solutions are compared with a low-cost filter that uses convolutional neural networks to detect edges at minimal computational cost, outperforming a comparable but more expensive method in feature extraction. The experiments also compare edge detection using Gaofen-4 and WorldView-4 satellite images, revealing distinct performance patterns due to differing image resolutions. High-resolution edges from the low-cost filter with Gaofen-4 and WorldView-4 images are combined to train a novel machine learning model for building type classification. Its incorporation of top-down segmentation and bottom-up recognition components, alongside local spatial features extracted by the low-cost filter, enables accurate semantic labels and the creation of building shape information. A comparative analysis of its performance with the more computationally expensive deep network-based solution and low-cost filter with Gaofen-4 and World-View-4 images demonstrates significantly lower error rates for all test datasets while requiring at least an order of magnitude fewer computational resources and a modest additional memory requirement. The novel classifier also outperforms the other methods in terms of accuracy, with a notable improvement of at least 2% and often up to 8% compared to the low-cost method, and may be applied to other high-resolution satellite images due to its robust performance across various test datasets. A semantic label creation method that uses a one-sided error-tolerant loss function achieves 100% precision and moderate recall rates, or high recall rates and moderate precision, depending on the specific application requirements. A unified framework is proposed to explain the non-linear, high-fluence X-ray absorption edge (XAE) through the diverse range of electronic excitation within matter. By considering multiple electronic levels and their individual charging states, each corresponding to specific raising probabilities, the complex spectrum can be broken down into its fundamental components. These fundamental components, influenced by the Fermi-Dirac statistic, are then subject to a non-linear transformation driven by the increase in absorbed photons. The resulting model effectively accounts for various factors present in the XAE and is in line with the principles of quantum mechanics. A theoretical calculation using the proposed model demonstrates a good match with the experimental XAE. This approach could facilitate quantitative analysis of XAE to determine the raising probabilities of different electronic levels. Furthermore, the proposed model can be applied to study a wide range of phenomena, such as short-pulse laser interaction with matter, X-ray optics, and Compton scattering. A related software package, dubbed "xae_rate," is available to model XAE and facilitate their quantitative analysis. The program is written in the Python language and is based on the existing "pylinx" framework. The model is characterized by three key rate parameters: the mean and standard deviation of the charging distribution, and the critical charging point. These parameters can be found through fitting of the model to experimental XAE. The proposed model is intended to serve as a versatile tool for the high-fluence XAE community. The theoretical calculation and validation of the model have been conducted at the Czech Academy of Sciences using the laser-plasma facility. The model is suitable for application in various fields, such as short-pulse laser interaction with atoms and molecules. The proposed approach may also be used to study the interaction of light with biological molecules and to create advanced X-ray optics capable of handling high fluences. The concept of comparison duals offers a new perspective on existing relationships between categories. This idea can be illustrated by examining the connection between posets and their order-dual frames, as well as the correspondence between functors and their right Kan-dual counterparts. Interestingly, comparison duals provide a unified explanation for the equivalence between the Gelfand and Naimark functors. This idea also serves as the basis for a generalization of Osoji's result regarding the duals of ordered monads. Furthermore, comparison duals are employed to formalize the relationship between posets and their duals, and the correspondence between functors and their right Kan-duals, among other results. Moreover, the concept of (U, V)-equivalence is introduced as a way to measure similarity between categories, and various examples of (U, V)-equivalent categories are given. It is demonstrated that comparison duals result in the equivalence of certain languages, and the relationship between category equivalences and language equivalences is explored. The concept of (U, V)-equivalence is applied to the study of formal languages. Moreover, the existence of (U, V)-equivalent categories with non-equivalent languages is demonstrated, and the concept of (U, V)-equivalence is applied to the study of formal contexts and corresponding Boolean algebras of subspaces. Finally, the concept of (U, V)-equivalent formal contexts is applied to the study of bimorphisms and to the calculation of the 2-magmas that correspond to these contexts. Calculations are provided for several prominent frames, including the atomic Boolean frame and the interval Boolean frame. Various theoretical models have been developed to comprehend the psychological phenomenon of the Sunk Cost Fallacy, where people persist in difficulties due to fear of loss. For instance, a structuralist approach has formulated the Sunk Cost Fallacy as a dynamical system and proposed a strategy to mitigate its negative consequences. Denial is a typical reaction to unappealing options, such as unpalatable meals. Children are initially inclined to deny, as their brains are still developing; however, as adults, this tendency subsides. Drawing from this concept, we've created a new argumentation mining objective that mimics denial, as part of a larger argumentation dataset called ArguAns. Our experiments show that existing models struggle with denial, much like how people reject unappealing meal options. To address this, we've developed new neural architectures based on Transformer, specifically 'choice-reduced' and 'choice-omitted' models that successfully handle denial. Our findings indicate that incorporating denial into argumentation mining leads to better performance when using reduced choice models, while a recent deepset.bert model performs better or similarly on typical sentiment classification tasks. The well-documented successes of attention-based models in neural machine translation have led to improved outputs, but they are often plagued by inconsistent performance and unpredictable fluctuations in translation quality. This is particularly evident in state-of-the-art open-source translation tools, where fluctuations can be severe enough to result in translated texts with errors. To mitigate these issues, this paper introduces a new approach, the "look-forward attention" model, which aims to produce more consistent translations by focusing on both past and future words within a sentence. The proposed model is based on an iterative mechanism where each word is translated in sequence, taking into account not only the preceding word, but also the preceding sequence of words. By looking ahead to subsequent words, this model is able to leverage context further along in the sentence, ultimately yielding notable improvements and superior consistency in translation outcomes, as validated across various languages and datasets. Furthermore, the paper also investigates how the "look-forward attention" model can be used in conjunction with existing attention-based models, and provides actionable insights into its implicit sentence-level reasoning process. The study's findings and analysis are made available to the community through the deployment of a state-of-the-art, production-ready neural machine translation library, known as "lookforward-mlmt". The latter is accompanied by high-quality pre-trained models, comprehensive experiment results, and thoughtful best practices. This work is released under the widely-used "Cosmoscentic" open-source license, a modular and easily-updatable software license. The paper's findings and resources (including lookforward-mlmt) are available at a dedicated website: lookforward-mlmt.com. A related project video can also be found at vimeo.com/197976830. Both resources are intended for long-term community engagement and collaboration. The study's website is still an active hub for development, but a new community initiative is being formally launched: the Lookforward Community Initiative (LCI). The LCI is a collaborative community that is being formed to ensure that the "look-forward attention" model and the software tools developed for this study continue to evolve and improve. The LCI's primary goals include (1) facilitating the maintenance and updating of existing models, (2) supporting the development of new language pairs, and (3) promoting an open and inclusive dialogue. Investors typically assess returns in relation to their existing wealth. The standard model assumes a specific orientation towards growth, with certain individuals however, exhibiting different responses to gains and losses. Given these unique preferences, optimal portfolios become more complicated to determine as they depend not only on an individual's attitude towards growth but also their intended level of growth. This study deviates from previous research focused solely on absolute wealth to a more comprehensive model that takes into consideration both absolute and relative wealth. By doing so, a more generalized equation for optimal portfolios is derived in the continuous case, along with its discrete-time equivalent. These equations serve as the foundation for two efficient algorithms for calculating optimal portfolios, suitable for both continuous and discrete settings. Our findings show that the traditional model is a special instance of this new framework and previous results provide optimal solutions for specific preferences but suboptimal results for others. Optimality is achieved by dynamically adjusting portfolio composition in response to changes in growth and intended growth, leading to a range of equilibrium states. The state of a portfolio can change either continuously or at regular intervals, leading to the concept of an optimal equilibrium path. The paper introduces a method for calculating this path, which may vary depending on factors. The proposed algorithms have been implemented in R and tested through various scenarios involving returns, with the intent of providing a practical tool for investors to analyze and understand the relationship between their desired level of growth and optimal portfolio composition. This, in turn, sheds light on the impact of an individual's growth orientation and intended growth on portfolio composition. The interaction between these two variables is found to be significant, indicating that optimal portfolio composition depends not only on an individual's growth orientation but also their intended growth. This is a key finding, showing that optimal portfolio composition is influenced by both risk aversion and expected returns. The proposed methods have been used to analyze how various variables affect optimal portfolio composition, particularly the impact of an individual's growth orientation and intended growth. The underlying code is now part of the R Econometrics Toolbox as the optimal.portfolio function, providing a practical tool for investors to understand the relationship between these variables. Text-video retrieval, an essential task in multimedia, has been simplified by the emergence of pre-trained 3D vision transformers that can quickly match visual data. Yet, existing methods typically rely on fixed short text representations that are embedded using the same pre-trained models used for visuals. This limitation hinders performance due to the considerable differences in nature between text and visuals. We propose a novel approach, TS2-Net, that involves a sophisticated token shifting mechanism to adapt text tokens from one embedding space to another. Additionally, a multi-head attention-based matcher is used to select key text tokens related to each video frame. Finally, a query-based encoder is employed to refine both the text and visual features. Experiments on three benchmark datasets showcase TS2-Net's superior performance compared to other methods. The associated code and models can be found at https://github.com/whwu1024/TS2-Net.

In the field of network science, referential attachment has been successful in explaining the formation of specific network patterns, particularly in social media and citation networks, by favoring existing nodes with greater attractiveness. However, its applicability is limited when explaining the creation of more generic networks exhibiting characteristics of real-world network properties. In contrast, uniform attachment methods generate more generic network properties, such as randomness and distribution of node connections. This study combines both approaches by creating a new model called directed hybrid random networks (DHRN), blending referential and uniform attachment mechanisms. As a result, DHRN produces a hybrid network with characteristics of being partially influenced by referential attachment and the rest by uniform attachment, thereby influencing the distribution of in-degree and out-degree in the network. By varying the mix of referential and uniform attachment, DHRN can produce a range of in-degree and out-degree distributions in the network. In particular, DHRN can generate power-law in-degree distribution and thicken tails in-degree and out-degree distributions for higher node ranks. These properties and their variation with the mix of attachment mechanisms have been numerically verified through simulations. Additionally, DHRN is compared with other established models, such as preferential attachment and thick tail models, in terms of its attachment mechanism and resulting network properties. This study contributes to network science by introducing a new model that can generate a range of referential and uniform attachment properties through the blend of two mechanisms. Further work aims to explore the applicability of DHRN to various real-world networks and simulate its growth to replicate the characteristics of existing networks. In particular, DHRN can replicate the network topology and degree distribution of Twitter by accurately replicating the distribution of in-degree and out-degree in the network for different mixes of attachment mechanisms. Moreover, DHRN replicates the network properties for a range of preferential and uniform attachment mechanisms used in existing models, such as preferential attachment and thick tail models. As a result, DHRN can replicate a wide range of referential and uniform attachment mechanisms and their resulting network properties. Existing methods, mainly based on classifiers, are capable of identifying interference from an established list of possible sources.  However, such approaches are inefficient when used in complex environments with numerous possible interference sources.  This paper outlines a novel method for simultaneously categorizing and quantifying interference using devices under test as sources, by training a Convolutional Neural Network. Our experiments involved classifying five types of interference from two devices under test, by training CNNs on data obtained from cross-correlation analyses. Specifically, we establish that a localizable measure algebra is locally normal if and only if it can be represented as the Glimm space of a countable type III$_\lambda$ factor, equivalently, if it aligns with a unique factorization of a tensor product involving a countable type I factor and a type II factor. We further demonstrate that unique factorization in this context corresponds to a specific condition involving equivalent bimeasures, requiring minimal cross-sectional interference. This condition is then generalized to a broader theorem involving positive operator limsup over an arbitrary collection of measures. In addition, we show that a localizable measure algebra with a topology satisfying certain locality conditions cannot be locally normal unless it possesses a specific, highly distributive property involving orthogonal elements. One consequence of this finding is that locally normal algebras cannot be dense within the lspace corresponding to a type II factor, unless the latter is of type II$_1$. Our research involves examining the recoil proton momentum at very low depths in deep inelastic scattering events with an emphasis on scattering elastic scattering.  We identify a novel observable in this type of scattering: the alignment of the recoil proton momentum relative to the direction of the incoming electron beam. This observable is independent of the photon's interaction details and is tied to the overall distribution of partons within the proton rather than the photon's interaction with a single parton. As a result, our proposed research goal is to investigate and analyze this new observable, known as the recoil proton alignment (RPA), and to explore its potential for yielding more precise insights into the proton's structure at very low depths within a scattering area corresponding to a scale of around 1-2 GeV. To achieve this, we create a customized, specialized database of parton density models for different types of distributions that extend from the ELASTIC scattering distribution up to a certain energy level, and to our knowledge, a number of different photon interactions with the proton that extend from the ELASTIC scattering distribution up to a certain energy level. We establish a statistical approach to determine the parton density models for very low depths (corresponding to a scale of around 1-2 GeV) based on the cross-section data from various experiments, and obtain the parton density models for very low depths (corresponding to a scale of around 1-2 GeV) of the parton density distribution of the proton. We discover that the RPA parton density distribution of the proton exhibits a distinct, non-linear trend in its distribution at very low depths (the trend is described by the $d_{u}ud_{d}d$ term) and we are able to identify the relationship between the non-linear trend in parton distribution at very low depths (denoted as $x$) and the square of the momentum of the recoil proton $t$ as follows: $d_{u}ud_{d}d \propto (1/x)(1/t^2)$$. Time series data in astrophysics often follow complex behaviors such as exponentials, logarithmic-spikes, or periodic patterns. Currently, there's no straightforward method to create Gaussian Process models that incorporate these features in an astrophysical context. Therefore, this paper introduces AstroGP, a Python package that provides simplified, intuitive ways to implement Gaussian Process models utilizing mature open-source tools. The package offers a range of kernels that mimic common astrophysical phenomena and we illustrate its usefulness with real-world applications from the field of stellar astrophysics. In particular, we showcase its effectiveness in modeling light curve data from eclipsing binary stars. The proposed approach provides a flexible, user-friendly solution that can be used to develop novel machine learning applications in astrophysics, as well as accommodate other complex time series data. Additionally, we reflect on the implications of the parametric nature of Gaussian Process models and how it affects model interpretability. interparticle potential and derived their excitation spectra numerically from the
Beltzer-Wirzviel scheme. Our analysis shows that a minimum repulsive interaction
is required for the Bose fluid's excitation spectra to conform to the Landau
series, as predicted by the central charge hypothesis. If this interaction threshold
is not met, the Bose fluid's excitation spectra display a Pauli obstruction,
characterized by a constant density of states along the zero-dimension of the
Borel-Chevalley fan. The emergence of the Pauli obstruction signifies a transition
from a Bose fluid to a quantum liquid, defined as a strongly correlated state of
Bose particles that conforms to the central charge hypothesis. Notably, the repulsive
interaction needed to trigger the Pauli obstruction in the Bose fluid is lower than
that needed to trigger zero-fermion degrees of freedom in a fermionic system. Our
analysis also reveals that the Pauli obstruction in the Bose fluid mounts a subtle
form of resistance against time-reversal symmetry, consistent with experimental
observations of repulsive Bose gases. The principles and concepts underlying

equations derived by Kheradmand et al. Our analysis also addresses a long-standing
uncertainty concerning the connection between the Beliaev equations and the

A new version of the multi-photon Monte Carlo event generator, KKMCee, is presented, which incorporates both lepton and quark pair creation processes. The latter offers considerable advantages in theoretical precision over previously used approaches. A detailed description is provided of the lepton and quark pair creation techniques in terms of helicity amplitudes within the soft photon phase space approximation. Furthermore, the generator is adapted to the HerWuD and Hi3G event generators, both of which utilize the multiple Z-boson resonance technique to simulate detailed photon spectra. As part of this project, theoretical improvements are also made to the standard Z-boson decay into lepton pairs. The KKMCee event generator also facilitates post-processing functionality to accommodate a wide range of hadronization models. An evaluation of its accuracy and photon spectral properties is conducted in preparation for future high-energy lepton collider research. At their core, embedding complex objects within lower-dimensional spaces enables the comprehension and analysis of intricate relationships within data structures that are topologically connected and dynamically changing over time. Despite significant advancements in static and temporal network learning, there is a notable neglect in the study of embedding evolving networks that require normalized representations, especially when dealing with objects like bicycles without a natural embedding space. In this research, we explore the possibility of embedding evolving graphs in fixed, low-dimensional spaces that capture temporal Network Characteristics. By developing innovative methods to establish alignments between the graph's temporal editions and guide the embedding, we leverage metric multiview learning to achieve our goal. Our approach is extensively evaluated using 14 diverse case studies across three categories: process discovery, multimodal learning, and transportation. Our findings indicate that the methodology we devised is effective in accurately embedding graph temporal editions by correctly establishing node and edge correspondence across multiple versions of the graph. Moreover, the resulting embedded spaces capture meaningful temporal relations and allow for the reconstruction of consistent multiview graphs. These results, in turn, enable the detection of anomalies, the discovery of processes from serialized data, and the construction of a combined transportation network. Moreover, we showcase the capability of our approach to learn and accurately place embeddings of objects that are not topologically connected, like bicycles. These results open up various applications in the domain of transportation. With the capability to monitor and identify irregular movements in the embedded space, we propose an anomaly detection approach and demonstrate that our methodology can be utilized to uncover biased law enforcement activities versus cyclists. Additionally, we present an innovative approach to uncovering the most effective routes in the embedded space, and show that the discovered processes and embedded spaces can contribute to various social and research endeavors. In the context of discovery, we are able to identify the most probable bike path based on the embedded spaces and, thus, develop strategies to minimize bicycle theft. These contributions not only expand the boundaries of learning temporal network characteristics but also provide valuable applications in the domain of transportation. Local tracing efforts, where groups of individuals help identify COVID-19 contacts of their neighbors, were a key component of the English contact tracing system.  To evaluate these collaborations, we studied the relation between the active local tracing groups in each English Metropolitan area and the local reproductive number (R), focusing on the time period between August 2021, when restrictions were fully lifted, and November 2021, a time when the COVID-19 vaccine was fully effective.  By modeling the impact of local tracing on R, we found that for every 100 additional local tracing participants, the reproductive number was reduced by 0.04 to 0.10.  Although we couldn't rule out that the observed reductions were caused by other factors, we concluded that local tracing may have had some additional impact on reducing the spread of COVID-19 in England.  Notably, if all Metro areas had maintained the low levels of local tracing volunteers observed in the last month of our study (approximately 30 per 100,000 people), this could have potentially avoided approximately 30,000 hospitalizations and 1,000 deaths.  Our study indicates that local initiatives such as collaborative tracing may be a valuable tool in future epidemic control and highlights the need to further understand their potential impact.  Importantly, our findings will likely be altered if the presence of local tracing volunteers were related to other factors influencing the spread of COVID-19, and future research should seek to identify and address any remaining confounding variables, allowing for a more precise quantification of local tracing influence.  To this end, we outline a set of potential future research directions to further explore the relationship between the active local tracing efforts and COVID-19 spread in future outbreaks.  Moreover, our results correspond to a particular scenario where the active local tracing volunteers were roughly proportionate to the population of the Metropolitan areas.  Consequently, our results might be subject to variation if the active local tracing volunteers were roughly proportionate to urban density or other factors.  Finally, our results might be altered if the volunteer structure of the tracing system was changed and would need to be re-evaluated in such cases.  Our results suggest that in the case of a future COVID-19 pandemic, enhancing local collaborative efforts similar to the Metro local tracing initiative could be a valuable strategy for reducing the transmission of an infectious disease.  Similarly, our results may be applied to other infectious diseases such as monkeypox, providing valuable insights into the impact of local collaborative efforts on reducing the spread of infectious diseases.
